articles.title: Australian coral reefs face risk of collapse within 50 years without drastic action, global assessment finds
articles.dek: Every shallow-water coral reef ecosystem in Australia faces an extremely high risk of collapse by 2075, driven largely by projected ocean warming, according to a global…
paragraphs: Every shallow-water coral reef ecosystem in Australia faces an extremely high risk of collapse by 2075, driven largely by projected ocean warming, according to a global assessment .

The assessment, a collaboration between the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), researchers at the University of Melbourne and more than 250 researchers around the world, found that 96% of the world's assessed coral reef ecosystems are now classified as critically endangered under the IUCN Red List of Ecosystems.

The study evaluated coral reef ecosystems in 127 tropical and subtropical marine ecoregions, including some of the world's largest and most biodiverse reef systems such as Australia's Great Barrier Reef, the Coral Triangle in Southeast Asia and the western Pacific, the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef and the Red Sea.
The assessment classified all 17 Australian coral reef ecosystems as critically endangered, with increasing marine heat stress and mass bleaching predicted under future climate scenarios.

Researchers found that climate-driven ocean warming is the most widespread and severe threat to coral reefs globally. Increasing marine heat waves are causing mass coral bleaching events and widespread coral mortality, placing ecosystems under unprecedented pressure.

Dr. Mishal Gudka, a University of Melbourne research fellow and scientific lead of the global assessment, said the risk of coral reef collapse is escalating, but this must be a wake-up call rather than a cause for despair.

"Coral reefs have shown a remarkable ability to bounce back from devastating bleaching events . Pockets of surviving, resilient coral reefs can remain in the future—but we must do everything within our reach to set them up for success," Gudka, from the School of Agriculture, Food and Ecosystem Sciences, said.

"Our assessment shows that much of the risk is driven by projected changes that have not yet fully materialized, and now is a critical window to scale up conservation and climate efforts to avoid catastrophic loss."

Dr. Ben Fitzpatrick, Oceanwise Australia director and adjunct research fellow at the University of Western Australia's Oceans Institute, who led the assessment on Australia's coral reef ecosystems, said although Australian coral reefs can respond well to local management, these gains are increasingly being overwhelmed by our changing climate.

"Unfortunately, these climate change impacts are only expected to intensify under current climate change trajectories, making the risk of collapse for all our coral reefs exceptionally high," Fitzpatrick said.
"If we double down on local management and achieve rapid decarbonization, we can avoid this outcome, but the window for action is rapidly closing."

Despite covering less than 1% of the ocean floor, coral reefs support around a quarter of all marine species. They provide habitat, food and breeding grounds for thousands of species while supporting fisheries, tourism and coastal protection for millions of people worldwide.

articles.title: Supercurrent enables the reading of quantum information without destroying it
articles.dek: One of the fundamental challenges of quantum computing is obtaining information from a quantum bit, or qubit.
paragraphs: One of the fundamental challenges of quantum computing is obtaining information from a quantum bit, or qubit. Unlike a conventional bit, which can be read repeatedly without altering its content, direct measurement of a quantum system typically causes the state to collapse before it can be determined. In other words, reading the information modifies it.

A new study proposes circumventing this problem by using a unique property of a certain type of qubit called an "Andreev qubit." This qubit produces an oscillating electric supercurrent through its own quantum dynamics. This supercurrent would serve as a macroscopic indicator of the qubit's state, enabling its reconstruction in a virtually nondestructive manner.

The study was published in the journal Physical Review B and was led by José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil, and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. According to the authors, this method could eliminate the need for ancillas, auxiliary qubits used in current techniques for nondestructive quantum readout.

Qubits are the fundamental units of information in quantum computers. While a classical bit can only be 0 or 1, a qubit can exist in various superpositions of these two states. This property gives quantum computing some of its most powerful characteristics but also makes the information extremely vulnerable to interaction with the environment and the measurement process itself.

"In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained," says Egues.

To overcome this difficulty, "quantum nondemolition measurements," or QND, were developed. In many of these protocols, the qubit's information is transferred to an auxiliary quantum system called an ancilla. The word "ancilla" comes from Latin and means "slave" or "servant." Today, figuratively speaking, the term is used to refer to something that serves another thing. In this case, measurements are taken on the ancilla to preserve the original qubit as much as possible.

While the procedure is effective, it requires preparing the ancillas, coupling them to the qubit, transferring the information and performing successive measurements, which can be time-consuming. In systems with many qubits, this additional infrastructure can represent considerable experimental overhead.
"Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself," says the researcher.

The qubit under study is an "Andreev qubit." It is named after the Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939–2023), who, in 1964, described a quantum process characteristic of the interface between normal and superconducting materials. These states, known as "Andreev states," are produced by this process and confined to the nanoscale region separating two superconducting materials. They can be used to encode the basic states 0 and 1, as well as their superpositions.

"In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot—that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined—formed in an indium arsenide [InAs] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It's in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed," Egues explains.

One property of this system is the circulation of a "supercurrent." This is an electric current that flows without resistance. The study showed that when the qubit is in a superposition of its basic states, the supercurrent exhibits an oscillating component over time. This oscillation, produced by quantum interference between the states that comprise the superposition, carries information about the qubit's state. "It's precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It's that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal," the researcher points out.

articles.title: Crows make decisions twice as fast as humans and monkeys
articles.dek: University of Tübingen researchers have shown that crows, when confronted with a visual choice, make a decision twice as fast as humans and monkeys.
paragraphs: University of Tübingen researchers have shown that crows, when confronted with a visual choice, make a decision twice as fast as humans and monkeys. In the experiment, two carrion crows took just 235 milliseconds on average to identify the direction in which a dot pattern was moving and to indicate their choice—while maintaining a high degree of accuracy.

Philipp Schmidbauer and professor Andreas Nieder from the Institute of Neurobiology of the University of Tübingen demonstrated how this speed is reflected in the activity of neurons in the crow brain. Their study has been published in the journal Science .

In the task, the birds had to determine whether moving dots on a touchscreen were predominantly moving to the left or to the right. The crows indicated their decision by pecking at a target to the left or right of the dot pattern. "Even when the patterns of motion were hard to recognize, the crows' decisions were still better than random choices," Schmidbauer reports, "and with clear signals, they achieved an accuracy of nearly 100%."

To investigate this ability, the researchers recorded the activity of neurons in the nidopallium caudolaterale, a key associative region of the avian brain, comparable to the prefrontal cortex in humans. As early as 70 milliseconds after the onset of the visual stimulus, neuronal signals for different motion directions began to diverge in the crows' brains—long before the birds could make their responses.

Neural activity gradually increased as the decision was being formed, until it reached a decision threshold and the crow indicated its choice. The neurons reflected both the strength of the available visual information and the direction selected.

"These findings show that neuronal dynamics in the avian brain are consistent with established models of decision-making in humans and nonhuman primates," says Nieder. Although birds do not possess a layered cerebral cortex, their differently organized brains appear to implement comparable basic principles of decision-making—and to do so twice as fast as primates.

This speed may be related to the evolutionary demands for rapid visual processing and motor responses in birds, Nieder explains. "Birds rely on their vision to carry out precise, rapid maneuvers during flight and to guide their beaks toward objects when foraging," he says, adding that further research will be needed to determine exactly which mechanisms enable this temporal advantage.

articles.title: Storms batter Europe, hitting power supplies, flights and phones
articles.dek: Storms battered northern Europe on Sunday, cutting power to more than 150,000 homes, forcing the cancellation of hundreds of flights and silencing phone networks.
paragraphs: Storms battered northern Europe on Sunday, cutting power to more than 150,000 homes, forcing the cancellation of hundreds of flights and silencing phone networks.
Winds of up to 84 miles (135 kilometers) an hour were recorded in Argyll and Bute in western Scotland, and fallen trees and power cables blocked roads and rail lines across the country.

More than 82,000 homes in Britain, nearly 60,000 in France and at least 10,000 in Germany had power cuts inflicted by the passage of storms Boelo and Austen within 24 hours of each other, authorities in the countries said.

Britain's Energy Networks Association indicated that more than 400,000 homes had lost power at some stage during the storms. Part of the pier at Brighton on the southern England coast, unused since a fire in 2003, blew away in Storm Austen on Friday.

The powerful winds also battered northern France across the Channel as Europe battled its first big autumn storms of the year and experts warned of more extreme weather events because of global warming.
French energy company Enedis said that at the peak of Storm Austen on Saturday, some 288,000 homes had no electricity.
Some 59,000 remained without power at midday Sunday, mainly in Normandy and Brittany. It said 2,600 Enedis technicians and contractors were working to reestablish power.

In Germany, Austen cut power to 10,000 homes in and around the southwestern town of Friburg-Brisgau on Sunday. The town's main hospital said it had to limit service to emergency cases because of the blackout that also cut the mobile phone network.
Two people were seriously hurt Saturday by scaffolding blown away by Storm Austen's winds during an autumn market at the town of Nastatten, German police said.
Germany's DWD weather agency predicted more powerful winds of up to 100 kph (60 mph) on the northern coast on Sunday.
The storms also hit the Netherlands and Belgium, where falling trees injured four people in Brussels on Saturday.
Hundreds of flights were canceled or diverted because of the storms across northern Europe.

Amsterdam's Schiphol airport, one of Europe's busiest hubs, canceled dozens of flights Sunday. AFP counted some 90 flights canceled on the airport website, mainly to European cities including Paris, Rome and Dublin. Dozens of flights due to land at the airport were also canceled.
Flights in northern England and Scotland were also hit by the storms.

articles.title: Monarchs report their locations via… cellphone?
articles.dek: Who knew a monarch butterfly could borrow a cellphone to check in with friendly people he met on his journey?
paragraphs: Who knew a monarch butterfly could borrow a cellphone to check in with friendly people he met on his journey? That is essentially what happens now that new technology has reduced the weight of a radio-pulse tag to less than half a gram (0. 02 ounces).

Those tags use Bluetooth technology to send information back to the researchers in the U. S. and Canada, including Jennifer Weber, Ph. D. '25, and Shawn Kurtzman from the Conservation Management Institute, allowing them to collect far more data than has ever been available about the paths and speeds of monarch butterflies as they migrate from a vast range in the continent's temperate areas to nature preserves in Mexico and Central America.
International calls are welcome, as some of the butterflies tagged in Virginia are now in Mexico.

Weber gave some of the monarchs names and keeps up with their perilous migratory journeys. Sneezy, tagged here in the New River Valley in September, was detected in Mexico on Oct. 17. Addison and Sleepy, also part of the mountain cohort, checked in from Texas but now seem to be traveling outside the range of cell service. Two other recent visitors to Virginia Tech, Hahn and Sandman, are now in Alabama and South Carolina, respectively. Orion and Walker were in Georgia, dealing with Tropical Storm Isaias, before heading west again.
Thomas is the real traveler. Tagged at Fort A. P. Hill near Fredericksburg, he was last detected in Mississippi, then pinged again 1,000 miles (1,600 kilometers) away in southern Mexico.

"We figured he would follow the Gulf Coast and make his way to the wintering grounds," Weber said. "Imagine our shock when he pinged yesterday at lunchtime all the way across the gulf. His latest ping put him a little bit east of a city named Coatzacoalcos, well south of the wintering grounds."
Weber said Thomas and a few other radio-tagged monarchs were picked up by a swirling storm system and deposited on the Mexican coast.

To say monarchs are checking in with cellphones is not hyperbole. The new tags emit a pulse detectable by Bluetooth-enabled smartphones, vehicles and cellular towers, which send a signal through a background function to the researchers to create a continuous, real-time map.
"It's citizen science , but crowd-powered," Weber said.

No information about the device itself is sent—just the tag number and location. It also means a monarch flying over wilderness could go days without being located, leaving Weber to wonder whether the tag stopped working or fell off, or whether the butterfly perished.
Kurtzman said the estimated survival rate is 25% to 28%.

Following a flight path at hundreds of data points reveals micro-level behaviors, such as whether monarchs use highway corridors, how they react to major weather disruptions and where they pause to feed on available nectar along their route.

Weber and Kurtzman outfitted 35 monarchs with pulse tags and follow their paths to winter quarters. The cost of the radio-pulse tags is still high enough that most butterflies are tagged with a small sticker on a wing that includes contact information for anyone who finds it. This message-in-a-bottle strategy returns data from a tiny percentage of monarchs.

The CMI researchers tagged monarchs on federal land around military installations in three Virginia locations—the Radford Arsenal for a mountain population; Fort A. P. Hill for a Piedmont population; and Oceana Naval Air Station and Joint Base Langley-Eustis to identify a coastal population. Monarchs tagged on the Tech campus were included in the mountain cohort.

articles.title: Milky Way's disk grew 'upside down,' with younger stars forming in ever-thinner layers
articles.dek: The Milky Way is home to hundreds of billions of stars arranged in a glorious spiral pattern. But beyond the obvious spiral, our galaxy has other physical characteristics.
paragraphs: The Milky Way is home to hundreds of billions of stars arranged in a glorious spiral pattern. But beyond the obvious spiral, our galaxy has other physical characteristics. It's divided into a galactic bulge, a galactic disk and a galactic halo.
The disk is further divided into a thin disk and a thick disk. They're not only structurally different, but their stellar populations and other characteristics are different.

The thin disk contains young stars and middle-aged stars like our sun. It holds the spiral arms, where our solar system resides, and most of the Milky Way's gas and dust. It's also where young stars form. It has higher metallicity, generated by previous generations of stars that have lived and died.

The thick disk is puffier and more diffuse than the thin disk. It holds ancient stars, and almost no new stars form there. It has much lower metallicity than the thin disk, and astronomers sometimes refer to it as a kind of stellar fossil record.

Astronomers wrestle with understanding the formation of these disks and the Milky Way as a whole. Observations have led to multiple explanations. In one, stars are born in the thin disk, and over time, encounters with gas clouds, the spiral arms or even the central bar perturb some of these stars. Dynamical scattering drives them away from the plane of the thin disk.

Another explanation says that as stars form in the inner disk, the gas they form from settles down into an even thinner disk. In this scenario, each successive generation of stars forms in an increasingly thin disk.

Astronomers have difficulty distinguishing between these competing explanations. Doing so relies on accurate measurements of the ages of individual stars. That's difficult to achieve, especially for the oldest stars.

New research in The Astrophysical Journal Letters used Gaia data to tackle the issue. It's titled " A Two-stage Settling of the Milky Way Disk Revealed by Precise ChronoGal Ages ," and the lead author is David Mirabal. Mirabal is a predoctoral researcher at the Instituto de Astrofisica de Canarias (IAC).

"The spatial distribution of galactic disk stars of different ages and metallicities encodes its dynamical evolution history and formation pathways," the authors write in their research letter. "The lack of precise ages for large, representative samples of stars has traditionally been a drawback for securely differentiating among formation scenarios proposed to explain the vertical properties of the Milky Way disk."

This work is based on data in Gaia Data Release 3 (DR3), released in June 2022. This paper is one of several released by a collaboration of researchers aimed at deciphering stellar ages in the populations of the thin and thick disks. In this one, the authors employed color-magnitude diagram fitting of the Gaia data. From that, they derived age-metallicity distributions for the stellar populations. They also studied their vertical profile—their position in either disk.

Earlier in the universe's history, the gas in the Milky Way was more turbulent and the galaxy was more puffed up vertically, as if it were one thick disk. Stars were born orbiting in the thick disk. As the gas calmed over time and became less turbulent, it cooled and shrank, creating a thinner disk inside the thick disk.
There was a significant change about 10. 8 billion years ago, a couple of billion years after the Big Bang, as the thin disk formed, with the older stars maintaining their orbits in the thick disk.
The existence of a clear break in the process about 10. 8 billion years ago is the main argument in this research. The rate of vertical settling changed drastically at around this time.

articles.title: How screening tools measure disadvantage may leave rural communities overlooked for public support
articles.dek: Whether a community is prioritized for public support can depend on how its needs are measured, according to new research from the University of New Hampshire.
paragraphs: Whether a community is prioritized for public support can depend on how its needs are measured, according to new research from the University of New Hampshire. The study found significant differences in how government screening tools identify communities, particularly in rural areas where those differences could affect access to funding.

Researchers compared four environmental justice screening tools, which use data on factors such as income, pollution and health to identify communities that may need additional public support. Three were developed by the White House, the Department of Energy (DOE) and the Department of Transportation (DOT), while the fourth was developed by New York state.

Nationally, the DOE tool designated about 18% of census tracts as disadvantaged, compared with about 35% for the White House and DOT tools. In New York state, more than half of census tracts (51. 3%) were identified as disadvantaged by at least one of the four tools, but only about 14% were identified that way by all four.

"We expected some differences, since each agency has its own mission. What surprised us was how large they were and how often they came from choices that aren't obvious from the documentation," said Qingran Li, assistant professor of economics at UNH's Peter T. Paul College of Business and Economics.
"The tools also disagreed more for rural communities, where resources tend to be more constrained, and investment may have historically lagged."

The study , published in Nature Communications , was conducted by Li; Stephen Bird, director of UNH's Carsey School of Public Policy; Susan Powers of Clarkson University; and Thomas Robbins of Schneider Electric.

Urban areas were more consistently identified as disadvantaged across the four tools. The DOE tool did not designate any rural New York census tracts as disadvantaged, while New York's own tool identified the greatest number of rural and suburban communities.

The researchers note there is no single formula for measuring disadvantage. Screening tools can consider factors such as income, health, transportation access, environmental conditions and climate risks, but they don't necessarily use the same factors or assign them the same weight.

They also differ in whether a community is compared with others nationwide, within its state or within its region. New York's tool, for example, accounts for regional differences, making it more likely that less urbanized communities are identified as disadvantaged.

"One of the things we saw in some of the federal tools is that rural areas often are not highly prioritized, in part because environmental problems are diffuse, but the economic vulnerabilities in those areas are very real," Bird says.
The findings also offer lessons for states like New Hampshire, where rural communities face challenges similar to those in New York's North Country, Bird notes.

"Many rural burdens look different from urban ones, such as long distances with limited transportation options, an aging population, high heating costs and reliance on fuel oil or propane. Tools built mainly around urban pollution, or around income measured against national or statewide benchmarks, may not fully capture those conditions," Li says.

"For example, a rural New Hampshire town with moderate incomes but very high energy costs and long drives to health care services could be designated disadvantaged by one tool and not by another. That could affect its eligibility for weatherization, clean energy or transportation funding."

articles.title: Scientists Develop a Clever New Way To Kill Cancer Cells From the Inside
articles.dek: Scientists have developed an experimental strategy that exploits a chemical byproduct of cancer cells to produce anticancer drugs directly inside them.
paragraphs: Scientists have developed an experimental strategy that exploits a chemical byproduct of cancer cells to produce anticancer drugs directly inside them.

Scientists in Japan have developed an experimental method that uses a chemical produced by cancer cells to manufacture anticancer drugs directly inside them. The approach relies on carbon monoxide, a toxic gas that certain tumors produce in unusually high amounts, to activate a chemical reaction designed to destroy cancer cells while limiting damage to healthy tissue.

In a proof-of-concept study published in Nature Communications , researchers at the RIKEN Pioneering Research Institute (PRI) demonstrated that their system could generate drug compounds selectively in cultured cancer cells. The findings suggest a possible alternative to conventional chemotherapy, although the technique has not yet been tested in animals or humans.

Carbon monoxide is best known as a poisonous gas released during incomplete combustion, including in vehicle exhaust. However, the human body also produces small amounts of it naturally. Research has shown that many types of cancer cells generate elevated levels, creating a chemical difference that could potentially be exploited for targeted treatment.

A team led by Katsunori Tanaka investigated whether this excess carbon monoxide could serve as a raw material for producing anticancer compounds inside tumors. Their strategy uses palladacycles, organometallic compounds containing palladium, to convert carbon monoxide into a molecule called phenanthridinone. Certain phenanthridinone derivatives are toxic to cells and have been used in anticancer drugs.

The researchers faced a significant obstacle: palladium catalysts are rapidly deactivated by substances naturally present inside cells, including glutathione. Without protection, the catalyst would lose its ability to carry out the drug-producing reaction.

To solve this problem, the team enclosed a palladacycle within albumin, an abundant protein found in blood. Albumin acts as a protective carrier, shielding the palladium catalyst from molecules that would otherwise disable it. The resulting albumin complex can circulate through the bloodstream and remain chemically active after entering cells.

After screening several palladacycles to identify the most effective candidate, the researchers tested the protected complex against human liver, cervical, breast, and lung cancer cell lines, along with a noncancerous cell line.

Following 48 hours of incubation, the researchers detected the intended phenanthridinone product in all four cancer cell lines but not in the noncancerous cells. The results indicated that the protected catalyst remained functional and that the reaction depended on chemical conditions associated with the cancer cells.

The team then refined the system to allow the newly synthesized compound to separate from its carrier and move freely within the cell. Further modifications enabled the production of a highly toxic phenanthridinone derivative used in anticancer drugs. When tested in liver cancer cells, the modified system generated the toxic compound internally, causing harmful effects in those cells.

Another concern was whether carbon monoxide already present in blood might activate drug production before the complex reached a tumor. Blood tests showed no detectable formation of the toxic compound. The researchers suggested that carbon monoxide bound to hemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying protein in red blood cells, was unavailable to participate in the reaction.

Rather than administering a finished anticancer drug, Tanaka’s approach aims to deliver relatively harmless chemical components that become toxic only after encountering suitable conditions inside diseased cells.

“This work represents an important advance in therapeutic in vivo synthetic chemistry,” says Tanaka. “In our therapeutic strategy, molecules naturally present or generated within the body—including disease-associated metabolites—are used as endogenous chemical feedstocks to synthesize therapeutic molecules directly at the site of disease.”

The researchers’ next step is to test the method in animal models, where they can investigate whether the catalyst reaches tumors, produces sufficient amounts of the drug, and avoids damaging healthy tissues.

articles.title: Patterns of polar vortices discovered in lead-free superlattices on silicon
articles.dek: A team at HZB has, for the first time, reported polar vortices in (BaTiO₃/SrTiO₃)₁₀ superlattices on silicon.
paragraphs: A team at HZB has, for the first time, reported polar vortices in (BaTiO₃/SrTiO₃)₁₀ superlattices on silicon. These results expand the range of materials and substrates on which polar topological textures can occur and open up new options for incorporating complex ferroelectric states into silicon-based technologies.

Polar textures such as vortices have so far been observed almost exclusively in lead-containing superlattices comprising ultrathin ferroelectric and dielectric titanate layers on oxide substrates. The delicate balance between electrical forces, mechanical stresses (imposed by the substrate) and the energy required to change the direction of polarization leads to distinctive electrical dipole patterns in the ferroelectric layers.

In principle, structures with complex polar states could be used to develop novel components with specific functions, as the structures are small, stable and can be influenced by external electric fields. However, to achieve this, it would be important to replace the toxic lead and deposit the layers on silicon substrates, the ubiquitous platform of the semiconductor industry.

A team led by HZB physicist Dr. Catherine Dubourdieu has succeeded in doing so: In its new study, published in Nature Communications , the team presents epitaxially grown alternating layers of barium and strontium titanates on silicon that exhibit regular stripes of polar vortices.

The layer system was created with molecular beam epitaxy in the HZB Quantum Materials lab. Using the scanning transmission electron microscope from the group of professor Christoph Koch at Humboldt University and further analysis at the PETRA III X-ray source in Hamburg, they were able to demonstrate the superstructure consisting of regular ferroelectric vortex tubes.

The vortices in each BaTiO₃ layer align along a specific crystal direction of BaTiO₃ and form a robust striped pattern. The silicon substrate provides the necessary mechanical strain, which enables the polar vortices to form. When the samples are heated, a structural phase transition occurs and the polar texture disappears. Upon cooling to room temperature, the polar texture reforms.

Phase-field modeling performed by the group of professor Long-Qing Chen at the Pennsylvania State University, U. S. , replicates the coupling of BaTiO₃ and SrTiO₃ layers via electrostatic forces and mechanical strain. This modeling also explains how the vortex tubes in the BaTiO₃ layers align, providing insight into the development of the polar texture pattern as a function of strain.

"This is the first realization of periodically ordered vortices in BaTiO₃ superlattices on silicon. Actually, silicon is the key, as it provides the necessary strain to induce this vortex pattern," says doctoral student Valentin Hevelke, first author of the study.

"Our results expand the range of materials and substrates on which polar topological textures can occur and open up new options for incorporating complex ferroelectric states into silicon-based technologies," says Dubourdieu.

articles.title: A Single Enzyme Could Hold the Key to Treating a Devastating Brain Disorder
articles.dek: Blocking an enzyme’s production restored brain growth and healthy behaviors in mice engineered to develop Angelman syndrome, pointing to a possible treatment target.
paragraphs: Blocking an enzyme’s production restored brain growth and healthy behaviors in mice engineered to develop Angelman syndrome, pointing to a possible treatment target.

Children with Angelman syndrome begin to show difficulties with thinking and movement at around 6 months of age. The rare condition occurs in approximately one in 20,000 births and is caused by the absence of a gene normally inherited from the mother. Researchers know which gene is missing, but they have struggled to explain why its absence causes these problems, making treatments elusive.

Research in mice now points to a chain of events that connects the missing gene to a stress response that interferes with brain growth. A team led by Jason Yi, PhD, an assistant professor of neuroscience at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis , traced that response to a buildup of a normally harmless enzyme. The study was published in Nature .

The missing gene, UBE3A , produces an enzyme called ubiquitin ligase, which helps keep cells orderly by marking unneeded proteins for disposal. It is active throughout the brain and participates in 60 different cellular processes. Identifying which of those processes contribute to Angelman syndrome required narrowing that broad field of possibilities.

Yi and his colleagues developed modified cells in the laboratory with UBE3A deactivated, then looked for proteins that accumulated without it. They identified 23 candidate proteins whose levels increased. One stood out for its strong connection to ubiquitin ligase’s normal housekeeping function: asparagine synthetase, an enzyme that helps cells produce essential proteins.

In mice genetically modified to develop Angelman syndrome, elevated levels of asparagine synthetase activated the brain’s stress response. Yet the enzyme does not interact with the usual triggers for that response, and its overabundance does not otherwise damage the cell. The consequences instead arise indirectly, as the stress response sharply reduces protein production and growth.

“The neurons are tricked into thinking that they’re in stress when they’re not — that’s bad because they will then not grow normally,” Yi said, noting that most children with Angelman syndrome have smaller brains than their peers of the same age. “It’s a reaction from the brain trying to conserve resources to protect itself. It does suggest that there is a dysregulation in the brain we might be able to correct.”

Blocking the production of asparagine synthetase restored normal brain growth and healthy behaviors in the mice. The team had corrected a later step in the biological sequence set off by the missing gene, allowing healthy development to resume.

The study is the first to link an increase in asparagine synthetase to a neurological condition. It adds to evidence that an imbalance in proteins can contribute to neurodevelopmental disorders by triggering stress responses, even when the proteins themselves are not directly damaging cells.

Yi said medications could potentially target the stress response triggered by asparagine synthetase, but much remains to be learned before work on a possible treatment can begin. His team is investigating precisely why the enzyme activates that response, where in the brain the response is most active, and when during development medical interventions would be most effective.

“We still don’t know a whole lot about the disease,” said Yi. “We haven’t been able to identify all of the things that the missing gene is doing and rescue the things that it is not doing in Angelman’s syndrome. But I think our data are the most complete so far to begin answering those questions.”

articles.title: Just Two Days on a Vegan Diet Triggered Unexpected Changes in the Liver
articles.dek: Switching from a vegetarian to a vegan diet altered liver metabolism in mice within just two days, making glucose production and toxic waste removal less efficient.
paragraphs: Switching from a vegetarian to a vegan diet altered liver metabolism in mice within just two days, making glucose production and toxic waste removal less efficient.

Millions of people follow a vegan diet, excluding all animal-derived products. Plant-based eating is recommended in part for its environmental benefits, but the health consequences of getting all dietary protein from plants are not yet fully understood. For researchers, that raises a question about how the body responds when the source of its protein changes.

Scientists at the University of Geneva (UNIGE) investigated that question in mice, focusing on the liver, which helps maintain blood sugar and processes the components of dietary protein. Their study, published in Molecu l ar Metabolism , compared a lacto-vegetarian diet containing both animal and plant proteins with a vegan diet.

“In just two days, the mice fed an exclusively vegan diet showed less efficient glucose production,” explains Pierre Maechler, full professor in the Department of Cell Physiology and Metabolism and at the Diabetes Center of the UNIGE Faculty of Medicine. “Furthermore, their livers were less effective at eliminating ammonia, a toxic substance released during the breakdown of amino acids. A significant reduction in physical activity also suggests effects on the body as a whole.”

Proteins from plants and animals consist of amino acids, small molecules joined together like links in a chain. Their types and proportions differ depending on the food source, so changing protein sources gives the body a different mixture to process. Plant proteins naturally contain fewer branched-chain amino acids than animal proteins. Along with helping build the body’s proteins, these amino acids supply some of the raw material the liver uses to produce glucose and maintain sufficient blood sugar during fasting.

“Overall, a change in diet alters liver metabolism very quickly, but this effect is just as rapidly reversible,” emphasizes Maechler. “The body adapts within one to two days to even subtle changes in dietary composition and returns to normal upon the reintroduction of animal proteins.”

The combination of less efficient glucose production and ammonia removal pointed the team toward a liver enzyme called glutamate dehydrogenase, or GDH. Located in mitochondria, the structures inside cells that help process fuel, GDH connects protein metabolism with sugar metabolism. To investigate its role, the researchers compared two groups of mice lacking the enzyme in their livers. One group ate a lacto-vegetarian diet, while the other ate a strict vegan diet.

Without GDH, the mice eating only plant proteins developed a severe buildup of ammonia and impaired blood glucose regulation compared with mice whose diet also included animal proteins. This confirmed the enzyme’s essential role in the metabolic response to an exclusively plant-based diet.

The experiments were conducted in mice, so they do not establish that people would experience the same changes. They do, however, provide a way to investigate the physiological questions that accompany a change in protein source.

“In addition to the ethical and environmental considerations that often motivate a switch to a plant-based diet, there are also scientific factors relating to the physiological functioning of our metabolism that are worth being aware of,” notes Maechler.

For people following a strict vegan diet, the researchers emphasize choosing protein sources rich in branched-chain amino acids, such as nuts, tofu, and lentils, to support the liver’s metabolic functions. They place that consideration alongside the need to ensure an adequate intake of specific vitamins.
The work was funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation (#310030_192486 to P. M. ) and the canton of Geneva.

articles.title: Earth’s Magnetic Shield Is Rippling Unevenly – Scientists Have Uncovered the Cause
articles.dek: The solar wind can weaken the very waves it creates along Earth’s magnetic shield, simulations show, helping explain why some regions are more active than others.
paragraphs: The solar wind can weaken the very waves it creates along Earth’s magnetic shield, simulations show, helping explain why some regions are more active than others.

Earth’s magnetic shield protects the planet, yet particles and energy from the Sun can still find their way through. Along its outer edge, a constant stream of solar material brushes past, stirring up waves where the two environments meet. A new study led by researchers at the University of Oulu explains why those waves grow stronger in some places than in others, revealing how uneven this boundary can be.

The protective region created by Earth’s magnetic field is called the magnetosphere, while the stream arriving from the Sun is known as the solar wind. Their interactions help drive space weather. On Earth, the effects can appear as auroras, while strong solar storms can disrupt satellites, positioning systems, radio communications, and power grids.

The boundary waves are known as Kelvin–Helmholtz waves. Similar patterns sometimes appear in clouds, and related phenomena occur in the Sun’s atmosphere, along the edges of other planets’ magnetic fields, and in interstellar space. Around Earth, however, satellites rarely pass through the most active regions.

Those limited encounters have made it difficult to establish how the waves behave under different solar wind conditions, so the researchers used computer models of the entire magnetosphere to examine their formation.

“This finding grew out of a long process of thinking through what I was seeing. In 2020, when I was visiting NASA as a postdoctoral researcher, I noticed unusual simulation images of the magnetosphere. I later realized that they showed Kelvin–Helmholtz waves at the edge of the magnetosphere, and that the different behavior of the waves on different sides was part of the same phenomenon,” says Academy Research Fellow Lauri Holappa from the University of Oulu.

The models traced the uneven wave activity to the way the solar wind’s magnetic field meets Earth’s field. Rather than wrapping evenly around the magnetosphere, the solar wind’s field drapes asymmetrically around it. This draped field can dampen the waves, but its damping effect varies from place to place, allowing stronger wave activity in some regions than in others.
“Asymmetries in the wave motion at the edge of the magnetic field have been observed before, but now we were able to show how they arise,” Holappa says.

The strongest activity appeared in the winter hemisphere, which faces away from the Sun. Within that hemisphere, the direction of the solar wind’s magnetic field determined whether the waves were concentrated on the dawn side or the dusk side.

articles.title: Earth’s Ice Ages May Have Started With a Planet-Wide Ocean Domino Effect
articles.dek: New research suggests that cooling in the Northern Hemisphere may have triggered far-reaching ocean changes that helped drive Earth’s past ice ages.
paragraphs: New research suggests that cooling in the Northern Hemisphere may have triggered far-reaching ocean changes that helped drive Earth’s past ice ages.

Growing ice sheets in the Northern Hemisphere may have helped push Earth into past ice ages by triggering changes in ocean circulation thousands of miles away, near Antarctica. New research from the University of St Andrews identifies a possible mechanism connecting these distant regions, helping explain how the planet naturally reduced atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) as ice ages developed.

Scientists have long known that the Southern Ocean plays a central role in regulating atmospheric CO 2 . Changes in its circulation and sea ice can increase the amount of carbon stored in the deep ocean, contributing to the cooling associated with ice ages. But researchers have struggled to explain how expanding northern ice sheets could influence waters so far south.

The growth of massive Northern Hemisphere ice sheets begins with changes in Earth’s orbit that alter how solar energy is distributed across the planet. According to the new study, published in the Journal of Climate , these expanding ice sheets may set off a much larger chain of events by cooling nearby North Atlantic waters.

As those colder waters move through the global ocean circulation system, they can eventually reach the Southern Ocean. If the northern cooling is strong enough, it could alter circulation around Antarctica and promote conditions that allow more CO 2 to remain stored in the ocean rather than the atmosphere.
This proposed connection provides a physical explanation for how ice sheet growth in one hemisphere could help amplify cooling across the planet.

To test the hypothesis, researchers used computer simulations that cooled only the ocean’s northernmost latitudes (mimicking the effect of a large ice sheet). They then examined whether the temperature changes could travel south and alter Southern Ocean conditions in ways that reduce atmospheric CO 2 .

The results showed that cooling northern waters alone produced a substantial response. The simulated reduction in atmospheric CO 2 reached 74% of the reduction produced when the researchers cooled the entire planet.

The experiments support the proposed connection between Northern Hemisphere ice sheets and Southern Ocean carbon storage. However, they demonstrate that the mechanism is physically plausible in a model, rather than establishing exactly how much it contributed to individual ice ages in Earth’s past.
Lead author Dr. Madison Shankle, from the University of St Andrews’ School of Earth and Environmental Science, explained:

“Essentially, we’ve produced evidence of a plausible mechanism connecting these two far-flung puzzles pieces – Northern Hemisphere ice sheets and Southern Hemisphere ocean circulation changes leading to CO 2 drawdown – which has been a tricky thing to explain in our theory of Earth’s past ice ages. Our study takes the step of actually demonstrating them working in model simulations, which is a big step forward for this field.”

Ice age research has traditionally emphasized processes occurring around Antarctica, where ocean circulation strongly influences the exchange of carbon between the atmosphere and deep ocean. The new findings suggest that temperature changes in distant northern waters may also be an important part of that system.

Past ice ages provide natural examples of how carbon moves between Earth’s atmosphere and oceans over long periods. Understanding these processes can help scientists improve climate models and investigate how the global carbon cycle responds to changes in atmospheric CO 2 , including the additional carbon dioxide released by human activities.

articles.title: Antarctica’s “Doomsday Glacier” Could Raise Sea Levels Twice As Much as Scientists Feared
articles.dek: Even without further warming, Thwaites Glacier could contribute twice as much to sea level rise by 2100 as previously estimated, according to a revised ice sheet model.
paragraphs: Even without further warming, Thwaites Glacier could contribute twice as much to sea level rise by 2100 as previously estimated, according to a revised ice sheet model.

Thwaites Glacier in West Antarctica has been retreating and thinning rapidly, while satellites show substantial acceleration in its ice flow. Traditional ice sheet models have depicted slower movement, leaving scientists struggling to reconcile their simulations with the observations. The glacier lies in the Amundsen Sea Embayment, a sector responsible for roughly one-third of the Antarctic Ice Sheet’s mass loss.

A new ice sheet model developed by glaciologists at the University of California, Irvine and NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory projects that melting at Thwaites could contribute up to 30 millimeters, or about 1. 2 inches, to sea level rise by 2100. That is twice previous estimates, even without additional climate warming. The study was published in Nature Communications .

“Glaciologists have long based their assumptions of ice sheet dynamics on the ‘grounding line,’ a discreet, narrow and mostly stable demarcation where ice leaves the land and begins floating on water,” said lead author Mattia Poinelli, who was a UC Irvine postdoctoral scholar in Earth system science when the study was conducted. “We have come to acknowledge a different arrangement beneath Earth’s major ocean-terminating glaciers. Satellite observations demonstrate the existence of a ‘grounding zone,’ sometimes kilometers wide, where warm ocean water is reaching deep underneath the ice sheets and causing vigorous melting.”

Synthetic aperture radar readings from the Finnish ICEYE satellite constellation allowed the researchers to detect kilometer-scale fluctuations in this zone along the main trunk of Thwaites. The data indicate that seawater penetrates several kilometers beneath grounded ice and lifts it during tidal cycles. This flushes the underside of the ice with pressurized, warm seawater, which currents altered by climate change push toward the Antarctic coastline.

That contact with the ocean affects how firmly the glacier remains anchored to ridges on the seafloor. According to Poinelli, a NASA JPL research affiliate who is now a project scientist at UCLA, the study showed that grounding zone processes accelerate the glacier’s detachment from these stabilizing features, allowing faster ice flow and deterioration.

“The Thwaites main trunk is being temporarily stabilized by the Mouginot Ridge,” he said. “Once that ridge is unpinned, the glacier will continually retreat across a predominantly retrograde seafloor toward its next topographic high, the South Ridge.”
A retrograde seafloor slopes downward farther inland, so retreat would carry the glacier into deeper water before it reaches the next rise in the terrain.

The researchers calibrated their model against more than 20 years of observations. By including a grounding zone instead of a grounding line, they reconstructed changes in the glacier from the 1990s to the present that were four times as pronounced as those represented in traditional models.

Simulations incorporating a grounding zone 4 to 6 kilometers wide, or about 2. 5 to 3. 7 miles, predict a 60 percent probability that the glacier will lose its anchoring contact with Mouginot Ridge by the end of the century, Poinelli said. “When you factor in key physical processes and calibrate against historical observations, you gain a reliable pathway for narrowing uncertainty in projections,” he said.

“We have documented and quantified the impacts of climate change on our planet’s sensitive ice sheets for decades, but a mounting realization gained in recent years of what is happening on the undersides of glaciers like Thwaites is leading to an even greater sense of alarm,” said co-author Eric Rignot, UC Irvine professor of Earth system science. “Most projections up-to-present have struggled to match the rapidity of the mass loss because of missing physics; our new model with more complete physics is able to match the record and then produces projections that are twice larger than before. These results predict greater risk of and exposure for coastal flooding than anticipated in the coming decades.”

articles.title: Mysterious Brain Signal Linked to Several Schizophrenia Symptoms
articles.dek: Schizophrenia affects how people perceive their surroundings, organize their thoughts, and communicate with others.
paragraphs: Schizophrenia affects how people perceive their surroundings, organize their thoughts, and communicate with others. Although these symptoms are often studied separately, new research suggests they may be connected to a common disruption in brain activity.

In a study published in Science Advances , scientists identified changes in a brain rhythm known as beta-band activity that were associated with several symptoms of schizophrenia. Patients with the most pronounced changes also had greater difficulty processing sensory information, more disorganized speech, and more severe clinical symptoms.

Researchers examined brain activity in 25 people with schizophrenia and 25 healthy participants using high-resolution magnetoencephalography, or MEG. The recordings were collected at the McConnell Brain Imaging Centre at the Montreal Neurological Institute-Hospital (The Neuro). Participants completed a task involving the timing of sights and sounds, and researchers separately analyzed their speech for signs of disorganization.

Compared with the control group, participants with schizophrenia showed weaker and slower beta-band activity. These brain rhythms are involved in processes that help the brain interpret sensory information and coordinate responses to the environment.

“What struck us was that the same weakened brain signal kept showing up wherever we looked, whether patients were processing a sound, a sight or completing a movement,” said Hsi (Tiana) Wei, lead author of the study and a postdoctoral scholar in McGill University’s Department of Psychiatry and the Douglas Research Centre . “Seeing the same pattern across these different domains suggested there may be a common underlying process linking the symptoms.”

The results support the possibility that some schizophrenia symptoms arise from disturbances in how the brain constructs and updates its understanding of the world. Rather than representing entirely independent problems, difficulties with perception, behavior, and speech may share an underlying neurological process.

“This gives us early but compelling evidence that measuring the brain’s operations, especially how it builds and revises its own model of the world, may help us appreciate that there is a common thread behind the confusing array of symptoms we see in disorders like schizophrenia,” said Dr. Lena Palaniyappan, senior author of the study, Professor of Psychiatry at McGill University, and director of the Centre of Excellence in Youth Mental Health at the Douglas Hospital.

Palaniyappan believes that further research could eventually help clinicians identify young people who need additional mental health support before psychosis develops. “The very first sign of schizophrenia begins in our adolescence, but this often gets missed for a long time. If this finding is confirmed in larger samples, we may have a potentially useful method to identify who, among youth seeking help for mental health, needs extra support to prevent psychosis,” he said.

The study involved just 50 participants, and its findings establish associations rather than demonstrating that altered beta-band activity causes schizophrenia symptoms. The researchers also have not established whether measuring this signal can reliably predict psychosis.
“This is a first, modest-size study, and the associations with speech and clinical severity will need to be tested in larger independent samples before we can be confident in them,” Wei said.

If future studies confirm the findings, beta-band activity could potentially serve as a measurable indicator of brain dysfunction associated with schizophrenia. Wei also suggested that the signal may be worth investigating as a future treatment target, although its clinical usefulness remains unproven.
