articles.title: Scientists Discover That Ovaries May Be Doing Something Unexpected Decades After Menopause
articles.dek: Ovaries often dismissed as inactive after menopause may still shape how women age, with human tissue revealing inflammatory changes and molecular similarities to ovarian cancer.
paragraphs: Ovaries often dismissed as inactive after menopause may still shape how women age, with human tissue revealing inflammatory changes and molecular similarities to ovarian cancer.

Ovaries continue to change for decades after menopause, long after their role in reproduction has ended. In a study of ovarian tissue from 28 women ages 50 to 75, scientists found age-related shifts in proteins associated with inflammation, immune activity, and the structure of the tissue surrounding cells.
The research, conducted by scientists at Northwestern University and the Buck Institute for Research on Aging, was published in Aging Cell .

“In the ovary, we reach a point of no return with respect to fertility in which it’s no longer producing eggs, and I would venture to say most people assume those ovaries are just sitting there doing nothing, similar to the appendix,” said co-corresponding author Francesca Duncan, associate professor of reproductive science in medicine at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine. “But that’s what makes this study very different.”

To investigate what changes after menopause, the researchers looked beyond ovarian hormones to examine the tissue’s protein composition. Co-corresponding author Birgit Schilling, professor and director of the Mass Spectrometry Center at the Buck Institute, led the team responsible for that analysis. Spearheaded by Buck Institute staff scientist and Schilling lab member Mark Watson, the work used advanced proteomic technologies that can identify and measure thousands of proteins at once. The researchers analyzed 5,812 groups of proteins in normal ovarian tissue.

Human ovarian tissue is difficult to obtain, making the collection of 28 ovaries unusually valuable, Duncan said. Concentrating on a 25-year age range after menopause allowed the team to isolate differences within the postmenopausal years, rather than comparing young and old ovaries across an entire lifespan. The technology also made it possible to examine thousands of proteins in every sample.

“When we analyzed the data in multiple different statistical ways, what became clear across all these methodologies is that the ovary was not stagnant,” Schilling said. “In fact, over the decades, there were quite dramatic differences in terms of some proteins’ levels would go up with age and some proteins’ levels would go down, which tells us this organ is quite dynamic.”

Ovaries from younger postmenopausal women contained more proteins involved in maintaining cells and tissue structure. Older ovaries had more proteins associated with inflammation, immune activity, and the breakdown and rebuilding of the tissue around cells. The differences were greatest between women in their 50s and those ages 70 and older.

Some of the molecular patterns also resembled those seen in cellular senescence. In this state, aging or damaged cells stop dividing but remain biologically active and can send signals that affect nearby tissue.

“Our data points to progressive aging features in which the ovary appears to lose its original identity and ends up doing something different,” Duncan said. “We do not yet know if there’s ever a point in a woman’s life when this organ is no longer beneficial and it’s actually harmful. These results really point to the need to ask this question.”

Duncan’s group had previously found similar evidence of continued remodeling in postmenopausal ovaries of mice . She began both that research and the human study with expectations that the findings ultimately challenged.

“I was predicting that if we took a 50-year-old ovary, a 60-year-old ovary, a 70-year-old, an 80-year-old ovary, they would all look exactly the same, have no eggs, and basically be non-functional,” Duncan said. “The fact that across species we’re seeing this gives us confidence that this isn’t just some random event, but something truly meaningful is happening in the biology.”
Women now routinely live for decades after menopause, Duncan noted, making the ovary’s role during this long period increasingly relevant to understanding women’s health beyond fertility.

“The ovary is not just a reproductive organ,” Schilling said. “It really influences how somebody ages because it speaks to all these other organs, such as the brain, and also to the bone, and women after menopause experience often a lot of bone problems. So, we think there is a connection between all these organs.”

articles.title: Boo! Feeling scared on Halloween can be fun for children but can sometimes push their limits
articles.dek: Halloween is one of the few holidays centered around children.
paragraphs: Halloween is one of the few holidays centered around children. When else can students come to school dressed like astronauts, monsters and witches, or ring strangers’ doorbells to ask for candy?

Horror’s bloody images lurk in the shadows – from ghouls leering over people’s lawns to skeletons hanging from trees – whether invited or not. Thoughtful adults might wonder, what is the right amount of scary for a child?
As a professor of children’s literature, and a writer of children’s books , I turn to the great author and illustrator Maurice Sendak for a hint.

A child’s mother once told Sendak that her pre-schooler was terrified of his classic 1963 book “ Where the Wild Things Are ,” which brings the reader into the world of an imaginative child, Max, after his mother sends him to his room without dinner. Through his imagination, Max journeys to a world of fantastical creatures called Wild Things.
No matter how many times this mother read “Where the Wild Things Are” to her young child, he screamed.
“What are you, a sadist?” Sendak answered. “Read him something else.”
“Why,” he continued, “ would any one book be right for every child ?”

When considering the benefits and drawbacks of scary books to get in the spirit of Halloween, some possible choices come to mind, along with some reminders to both overly cautious and sometimes careless adults.

To start, Felicia Bond’s 1987 “ The Halloween Performance ,” later republished as “ The Halloween Play ,” is a perfect Halloween picture-book classic, appealing to all ages and offering humor and suspense.
Bond is the illustrator of the 1985 children’s best seller, “ If You Give a Mouse a Cookie ,” and subsequent books. An adorable young mouse features in this Halloween story, as well.
The plot revolves around a mysterious “small but important part” that Roger, a nervous, brown mouse, has landed in the school Halloween performance.
Costumed skeletons and witches don’t bother him – but his jitters about performing on stage do.
Roger overcomes stage-fright to shine in the school performance. He may inspire other children to overcome their own feelings of nervousness at Halloween and make fun memories.
Frog and Toad are Arnold Lobel’s beloved, amphibian best friends from his children’s series published in the 1970s.

Though they have very different personalities, both Frog and Toad enjoy the thrill of playing with fear. In “ Shivers ,” a story in the book “Days with Frog and Toad,” Frog tells Toad a tale about “the old dark Frog” who combs the woods in search of tasty children.
Toad keeps asking, “Is this real?” Frog answers like any good storyteller, “Maybe it is and maybe it isn’t.”
Together the duo enjoy scaring themselves into a teeth-chattering but delightful evening.
They show young readers that, in the right doses, fear can be fun: ask any kid scream-laughing on a roller-coaster.
In another story, “ Dragons and Giants ,” Frog and Toad test their own heroism after reading fairy tales about dragons and giants.
Frog and Toad are both fearful and brave, as most of us are.

Wise children’s stories reinforce the truth that it’s natural to be both, sometimes at the same time. “Frog and Toad” features color illustrations in subtle greens and browns, leaving enough space for kids to imagine new facets of themselves – the timid and the bold.
Fear is inevitably woven into the fabric of children’s lives.
Nightmares, for example, spring from unknown sources, though studies show they are intensified by trauma, emotional disturbances and exposure to violence .
Bad dreams – like scary stories – work as fire drills for the developing brain.

articles.title: NASA, Partners Accelerate Lander Development for 2028 Moon Missions
articles.dek: As NASA returns humans to the lunar surface and establishes a long-term presence on our closest celestial neighbor, the agency and commercial human landing system providers…
paragraphs: As NASA returns humans to the lunar surface and establishes a long-term presence on our closest celestial neighbor, the agency and commercial human landing system providers Blue Origin and SpaceX have streamlined the designs and changed both concepts of operations for its future crewed landers.

Since NASA established initial contracts with Blue Origin and SpaceX for crewed missions to the Moon, the agency has redefined Artemis III to demonstrate rendezvous and docking capabilities between test versions of landers from each provider and the agency’s Orion spacecraft in low Earth orbit next year. In parallel, the companies are also developing crew and cargo versions of their landers for near-term Artemis missions.

“We are executing President Trump’s National Space Policy to complete the long-awaited return of American astronauts to the lunar surface in 2028 and establish a Moon Base,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “We have a proven foundation in SLS and Orion, along with two lunar landers in development with Blue Origin and SpaceX. But NASA has no intention of sitting idly by as all the pieces come together. That is not how Apollo succeeded, and it is not how the near-impossible is achieved. NASA is energized, our core capabilities are being rebuilt, our machine shops are running 24/7, and our experts are in the field attacking the critical path.
We are building a Super Bowl-caliber team to safely achieve these objectives and everything that comes next.”

For the initial crewed missions to the Moon, Artemis astronauts will launch in the agency’s Orion spacecraft on top of the SLS (Space Launch System) rocket from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. During each Artemis mission, a commercial human landings system will link up with Orion before taking two crew members to the lunar surface while two remain aboard Orion. To accelerate development toward a 2028 landing, the Artemis landers and Orion will no longer rendezvous in a near-rectilinear halo orbit around the Moon and instead meet up in an orbit that differs for each partner, informed by their systems.

Both companies are required to perform an uncrewed demonstration mission with their crewed landers prior to the near-term Artemis crewed missions to the Moon. NASA will certify lander systems prior to the crewed missions to ensure safety and mission success.

SpaceX continues to plan for an in-space propellant aggregation approach to transfer super cold, or cryogenic, liquid propellant in space. The company will launch multiple versions of Starship to low Earth orbit prior to the launch of the Starship Human Landing System (HLS) from Florida. Similar to a gas station on Earth, the series of propellant “tanker” Starships in low Earth orbit will transfer propellant to the waiting “depot” Starship. The depot Starship will ultimately fuel the Starship lander for its journey to the Moon.

Under the revised operations, Starship HLS will await Orion and its crew in Earth orbit. The lander and Orion will rendezvous and dock in Earth orbit, then the Starship lander will perform a trans-lunar injection burn to send the combined lander and Orion stack to low lunar orbit. NASA is working to modify Orion to enable Starship to push it to the Moon. The lander will bring two crew members to the lunar surface for several days before delivering them back to Orion for the ride back to Earth.

Propellant aggregation in low Earth orbit allows for flexibility in the crew launch timing on SLS, while a trans-lunar injection burn performed by the Starship lander will enable direct access to low lunar orbit. This new concept of operations using low lunar orbit will significantly lower the amount of propellant Starship needs to aggregate in space while reducing the amount of time it can take for astronauts leaving the Moon’s surface in Starship to link back up with Orion. SpaceX will demonstrate the propellant aggregation approach during the uncrewed demonstration mission.

articles.title: NASA’s Artemis III Mission to Test Future Moon Lander Operations
articles.dek: Before astronauts return to the lunar surface, NASA will first conduct one of the most ambitious and complex test missions in the agency’s history.
paragraphs: Before astronauts return to the lunar surface, NASA will first conduct one of the most ambitious and complex test missions in the agency’s history.

Launching in 2027, Artemis III will send NASA astronauts Randy Bresnik, Frank Rubio, Andre Douglas, and ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Luca Parmitano aboard the Orion spacecraft into low Earth orbit to perform a series of demonstrations with test versions, or test articles, of human landing systems being developed by industry partners Blue Origin and SpaceX. During the planned 14-day mission, crews and flight controllers will practice the rendezvous, docking, habitation, and operational procedures that will be essential when Artemis astronauts begin landing near the Moon’s South Pole in 2028.
The mission is designed to reduce risk, validate hardware, and gain operational experience before NASA attempts a crewed lunar landing.

“Every piece of this mission in Earth orbit is designed to reduce risk before we put astronauts back on the Moon,” said Jeremy Parsons, NASA’s Artemis program manager. “We’re launching three spacecraft on three different rockets and testing how they operate together — something NASA has never attempted. Every lesson we learn here gets us closer to landing on the Moon in 2028.”

Earlier Artemis missions used only NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket and Orion spacecraft. Artemis III will involve three separate spacecraft launched on three different heavy-lift rockets within a relatively short period of time.

The mission begins with Blue Origin launching a test version of its Blue Moon Mark 2 lander into a circular low Earth orbit approximately 273 miles (237 nautical miles) above Earth. The spacecraft can remain on orbit for up to 30 days providing schedule flexibility. Artemis III is designed as a tightly choreographed campaign, with NASA planning to launch Orion on top of SLS from the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida only days after the Blue Moon test article launch and confirmation the vehicle is healthy and ready for joint operations.

Following launch, Orion will initially enter an elliptical Earth orbit of 18 x 1122 miles (16 x 975 nautical miles). It will use its service module to perform a series of maneuvers to transition to a circular orbit at about 345 miles (300 nautical miles) for thermal stabilization before then gradually setting up its rendezvous with the waiting Blue Moon lander test article. Because each spacecraft operates in slightly different orbital regimes optimized for its mission requirements, Artemis III requires a carefully choreographed sequence of orbital maneuvers and rendezvous operations throughout the flight.

During the first two days of flight, the crew will check out Orion’s systems, prepare for proximity operations, and gradually position themselves for the mission’s first major objective: rendezvous and docking with the Blue Moon test vehicle.

The operation represents NASA’s first opportunity to evaluate how Orion and a commercial lunar lander work together in space. Engineers will assess how software aboard both spacecraft, guidance systems, communications systems, and operational procedures perform in real-world conditions, while flight controllers gain experience coordinating activities across multiple teams and organizations.

Once docked, astronauts will spend approximately two days conducting evaluations aboard the Blue Moon test article. Crew members will open the hatch and enter the spacecraft, allowing them to assess the cabin environment, controls, and life-support systems firsthand. Teams will verify the spacecraft’s ability to maintain the proper atmosphere and pressure.

The Blue Moon test article incorporates many of the avionics, software, flight-control systems, crew-cabin technologies, and life-support functions planned for future lunar missions. Testing those systems in orbit will provide the first opportunity to evaluate how many of the lander’s flight systems perform in space as an integrated vehicle.

By the time Orion undocks, NASA will have completed its first evaluation of a commercial lunar lander with crew, gathering data on spacecraft systems, crew operations, and spacecraft interoperability not possible on the ground.
After completing operations with Blue Origin’s lander, Orion will undock and reposition to support the next phase of the mission: a second rendezvous operation.

articles.title: NASA’s Swift Mission Ends, Leaves Behind Scientific Bonanza
articles.dek: NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has ended its science mission now that the spacecraft is orbiting less than 171 miles (275 kilometers) above Earth’s surface.
paragraphs: NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has ended its science mission now that the spacecraft is orbiting less than 171 miles (275 kilometers) above Earth’s surface. The greater atmospheric drag at this height prevents the satellite’s telescopes from steadily gazing at their astronomical targets.
Swift conducted its final observation on Oct. 20. It is expected to re-enter the atmosphere in the next few weeks.

“Swift delivered an incredible, lasting return on investment for the nation, designed for a two-year primary mission but productive for more than 10 times as long,” said Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director, Astrophysics Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington. “In that time, Swift played a major role in advancing our understanding of the changing universe and was part of a revolution in astrophysics that showed how critical rapid-response observations are to the entire community.

To support rapid response to cosmic events in a post-Swift world, we’re exploring our ability to use and augment NASA’s fleet of existing space telescopes, from fast-to-orbit commercial capabilities to efficient, innovative new missions. And Swift leaves us with an extraordinary archive of multiwavelength observations that will fuel new discoveries for decades more.”

In its storied career, Swift has observed more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts , the most powerful explosions in the cosmos. It has studied more than 1,400 supernova explosions, witnessed stars shredded by black holes , monitored active galaxies , conducted an all-sky X-ray survey, studied asteroids and comets , and more. Swift data has contributed to about 7,000 published scientific papers.

“Swift was designed as a satellite dedicated to studying gamma-ray bursts, outbursts that came and went so quickly that no one could target them with large telescopes to learn more,” said S. Bradley Cenko, the mission’s principal investigator at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. “Swift needed to detect and locate gamma-ray bursts, communicate their position to other observatories, and then swing its telescopes around to image the burst locations before their afterglows faded out. This typically took Swift about a minute to do.”

Led by its first principal investigator, Neil Gehrels, Swift was born as a multiwavelength observatory, with co-aligned Optical/Ultraviolet and X-ray telescopes that could quickly image and refine a burst’s position. The mission launched into orbit on Nov. 20, 2004, and went to work the following month. In 2018, NASA renamed the mission to honor Gehrels following his death.

Speed was especially important for an elusive population called short gamma-ray bursts, which reach peak brightness in less than two seconds. Until Swift, it had been impossible to locate these bursts rapidly and precisely enough to observe their afterglows. In May 2005, Swift achieved this milestone with GRB 050509B , which lasted just 0. 03 seconds. Swift turned to the burst fast enough to detect 11 X-ray photons, making this the first short burst with a detected afterglow. These observations validated long-standing theoretical models, showing that short gamma-ray bursts likely come from mergers of two neutron stars — objects with the mass of the Sun that have been crushed to the size of a city.

Another factor led to Swift’s success as a kind of astronomical multitool. Its flexible planning system enabled astronomers to request “target-of-opportunity” observations that could be commanded from the ground in as little as a few minutes, or to set up monitoring programs for observing specific sources lasting from as little as a few minutes to months. The system could schedule up to 75 independent targets a day.

“The unique speed of response of the Swift hardware, the extraordinary success of the rapid mission operations, and the closely knit teamwork of the Swift Flight and Science Operations teams placed Swift at the crossroads of burgeoning areas of research,” said John Nousek, the mission’s operations director and professor of astronomy and astrophysics in the Eberly College of Science at Penn State in University Park, Pennsylvania.

The Swift archive contains nearly 22 years of brightness measurements of all kinds of cosmic outbursts, multiwavelength spectra, more than 1. 5 million images from its Ultraviolet/Optical Telescope, and much more. The full dataset, publicly available as part of NASA’s commitment to open, gold standard science, spans approximately 12 terabytes, the storage equivalent of about 600 high-definition movies.

articles.title: Ancestors all around – millions of dead people linger in Americans’ memories
articles.dek: Halloween kicks off a series of religious and cultural festivals to honor the dead, including All Saints’ Day, All Souls’ Day and the Day of the Dead.
paragraphs: Halloween kicks off a series of religious and cultural festivals to honor the dead, including All Saints’ Day, All Souls’ Day and the Day of the Dead. But deceased loved ones don’t disappear from people’s social worlds once the ghost and skeleton decorations come down.

Present in memory and tradition, the dead can shape people’s identities and behaviors long after they die. Recent survey data shows that almost 44% of Americans report that they have felt the presence of a deceased relative or that they have communicated with a deceased relative in the past year alone.

Researchers lack basic knowledge about this shadow population. As demographers , we typically study the living. But in our recent work, we asked a very unusual demographic question: What does a population of our deceased relatives look like?

Our research typically categorizes the living population by age groups and other demographic attributes. In our recent study, we took our analysis a step further to estimate the size and age distribution of the currently living population’s deceased relatives. We focused specifically on deceased grandparents, parents, siblings, spouses and children.

To do this project, we relied on a modeling framework called demographic microsimulations . This approach produces results only for Black and white Americans. The method cannot estimate relative populations living outside of the United States, so it excludes groups with high percentages of foreign-born individuals who have family abroad.
Our study focused on the populations as of July 2020, but for the purposes of this article, we updated our analysis and weighted results to the estimated population as of October 2026.

Because estimating the deceased relative population is not a common exercise in our field, we had to make some modeling decisions. We counted only deceased relatives who died after the birth of at least one person still alive; if no one remains who could remember them, we did not include them.

Also, we counted deceased persons based on how many relatives they have in the living population. For example, if a deceased 60-year-old man is survived by a spouse, an adult child, a grandchild and a sibling, we count him in the deceased relative population four times, reflecting his being remembered by four living individuals. As such, the deceased relative population we quantified is really a count of how many direct relative ties remain to those who are dead.

And finally, we classified deceased relatives according to their age at death. We believe this represents the age many people will most clearly remember their deceased loved ones. Of course, we categorize the living population by their current age.

First, the deceased relative population is large. Our model estimated that the living Black and white population representing about 217 million people , had 755 million ties to deceased close relatives . That’s a population more than three times the size of the living population. For every under-15-year-old out trick-or-treating on Halloween, there are about 21 deceased relatives remembered.

Second, our model shows that, on average, the deceased relatives died 25 years ago. That the average deceased relative has been remembered for a quarter of a century makes it clear that loved ones are often suspended in memory for years, even decades, after their deaths.

Third, over half of the deceased relative population was born more than 100 years ago – even before the term “trick-or-treating” took hold in the U. S . Around 10% of the deceased relatives were born before 1900, with 140,000 of them born before the Civil War – these are the remembered grandparents of today’s oldest individuals. These results speak to how generations of the seemingly long ago past still have a direct tie to the living.

The Halloween season reminds us of ghosts, spirits and ancestors. Whatever their beliefs, many Americans also carry relationships with people who are no longer alive: grandparents whose recipes they still make, parents whose advice they still hear, spouses whose absence shapes their days.

These relationships are deeply personal, but together they form a vast and previously unstudied shadow population. By quantifying and characterizing the deceased relative population, our research reveals just how many people no longer appear in the census yet remain an integral part of our social world.

articles.title: UN peacekeepers prepare to exit Lebanon after 70 years – leaving behind a worrying security vacuum
articles.dek: For nearly 70 years, the blue helmets of United Nations’ peacekeepers have dotted the landscape of southern Lebanon. But those days may soon be over.
paragraphs: For nearly 70 years, the blue helmets of United Nations’ peacekeepers have dotted the landscape of southern Lebanon. But those days may soon be over.
Under Israeli and American pressure, the U. N. Security Council unanimously voted in August to end the mandate establishing the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon, or UNIFIL .
It means the 7,565 members of UNIFIL deployed in Lebanon – representing about 46 countries – will depart the country no later than Dec. 31, 2026.

The end of the U. N. presence comes at a pivotal time. Israel and Lebanon have already held seven rounds of negotiations aimed at bringing a lasting peace to a region that has suffered from decades of conflict.

Brokered by the United States, these talks that led to the signing of the Trilateral Framework in June 2026 call for the disarmament of Hezbollah, the Israeli withdrawal from all Lebanese lands and the settlement of all disputes over borders. Yet all of these conditions are still some way off from completion – and beset by a series of barriers .

As such, the departure of the United Nations peacekeeping forces raises serious concerns. The potential for a security vacuum looms large in south Lebanon, especially given that Israel continues to bomb Lebanon despite a ceasefire that has nominally been in place since April 16, 2026 .

As a scholar of Middle East Studies , I know that UNIFIL has never been a permanent solution. But I fear that its termination creates more problems than it solves, especially when there are no clear replacements or post-UNIFIL security arrangements in place.
While the U. N. had had an on-the-ground presence in Lebanon to handle civil strife since the 1950s , its role in mediating between Lebanon and Israel started later.

In 1978, after a series of attacks on Israel organized by Palestinian fighters in Lebanon, Israel invaded and occupied the south in what was known as Operation Litani . As a result, the United Nations Security Council established UNIFIL to monitor Israel’s withdrawal from south Lebanon and to restore peace at the Lebanese–Israeli border.

Israel’s occupation of south Lebanon lasted more than two decades . Following its withdrawal on May 25, 2000, the U. N. set the Blue Line – a 75-mile (120 km) demarcation line created for the practical purpose of confirming Israeli withdrawal from south Lebanon. It was not an official border but a buffer zone monitored by the U. N. peacekeepers.
UNFIL and the Blue Line served as geographic and diplomatic focal points in the 2006 war between Hezbollah – an Iranian-backed militia operating from Lebanon – and Israel.

Resolution 1701 of the Security Council, which brought an end to the 2006 war, dramatically expanded the UNIFIL role in Lebanon ; the number of troops went from 2,000 to 15,000 authorized military personnel.

Its mandate also changed to include monitoring the ceasefire and documenting its violations, coordinating with Lebanon’s military and functioning as the only direct communication channel between the Lebanese and Israeli militaries. UNIFIL also offered humanitarian aid to the affected civilian population of south Lebanon.

Yet UNIFIL’s role never altered the basic lack of peace on the Israeli-Lebanese border. Over 50 years, Israel invaded Lebanon numerous times . And since 2000, Hezbollah has flourished in south Lebanon .

As UNIFIL prepares to depart, it’s unclear what will fill the looming security vacuum. It could be filled by non-U. N. troops, but Lebanon’s past shows the risks inherent to international peacekeeping missions.

In 1982, after Israel invaded Lebanon and occupied Beirut with the intention of eliminating the Palestinian militant threat, Lebanese authorities called on Western powers for help. In August, the governments of the U. S. , France, Italy and the United Kingdom created a multinational peacekeeping force designed to restore peace and stop the fighting between the Lebanese, Palestinians and Israelis.
But on Oct. 23, 1983 , the multinational peacekeeping force was the target of a dual suicide attack that killed 241 American service members and 58 French paratroopers.
To this day, the attack – claimed by the pro-Iranian Islamic Jihad – remains the deadliest single-day incident for the U. S. Marine Corps since the Battle of Iwo Jima in 1945.
In addition to Israel, interventions in Lebanon have also come from another neighboring country.

In 1976, the Syrian military intervened during Lebanon’s civil war to put an end to sectarian violence. Nearly three decades of occupation followed, and troops were withdrawn only following the assassination of Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik Hariri in 2005 and the subsequent Cedar Revolution .
With the absence of an internal Lebanese consensus, the arrival of any international peacekeeping force to replace the exiting UNIFIL will be perceived by many Lebanese as a top-down imposition.

Moreover, the situation on the ground makes it dangerous for any international force to successfully operate. Israel is reportedly occupying over 10% of Lebanon’s territories , including multiple permanent bases and outposts in southern Lebanese territory.
Finally, the fate of Lebanon-Israel direct negotiations is unclear . Recently, the countries held military talks in Florida, but little is expected from them .

Yet a number of efforts are ongoing despite the difficult circumstances surrounding UNIFIL’s withdrawal. On June 25, French President Emmanuel Macron and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni announced an “ international coalition to support Lebanon ” to reinforce Lebanon’s sovereignty and help prevent a security vacuum in south Lebanon.

articles.title: NASA, Virginia Launch Power Partnership for Energy Security
articles.dek: NASA is helping to foster long-term energy security in Virginia.
paragraphs: NASA is helping to foster long-term energy security in Virginia.

NASA’s Langley Research Center in Hampton, Virginia, is partnering with the Virginia Department of Energy to support informed decisions for effective energy generation, delivery and use by providing solar, meteorological, and future weather risk datasets for energy system modeling and planning purposes.

Under a new Space Act Agreement announced during a ceremony Friday, the partnership will use NASA expertise in atmospheric sciences to assist Virginia Energy in support of resiliency studies, resource analysis, and long-term energy planning.

“NASA Langley relishes the opportunity to put our unique science data into the hands of those who want to improve people’s lives,” said NASA Langley Deputy Director Allen Kilgore. “This collaboration with Virginia Energy will benefit the citizens of Virginia and provide stronger energy security for the Commonwealth.”

This agreement will help state officials plan for current and potential extreme weather conditions in Virginia and assess implications for electricity demand, energy generation, and system stress. Information can be directly incorporated into energy policy, planning, and operational decisions.

By helping Virginians better anticipate energy demands, prepare for extreme weather, and understand factors affecting electricity generation, this partnership will support a more reliable and resilient energy system.

“Sound energy planning depends on models that reflect real-world conditions,” said Virginia Energy Director Vince Maiden. “This collaboration will help us better understand how weather affects electricity supply and demand, identify vulnerabilities, and weigh resource tradeoffs with greater confidence.”

The partnership will infuse relevant NASA Prediction of Worldwide Energy Resources (POWER) data products into Virginia Energy’s modeling and analysis system. The POWER information supports energy generation system designs and prediction of energy production using validated data products from NASA’s Earth Science to Action program. Those key NASA products represent research and development across NASA including Langley, Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, and Ames Research Center in California’s Silicon Valley.

Through a digital pipeline, Virginia Energy can connect to Langley’s POWER web platform to download specific datasets and put them directly into their modeling tools. NASA’s POWER team members will work with Virginia Energy researchers to streamline the exchange, adjust formats, and evaluate the need for additional data.

This new partnership was fostered through NASA Langley’s Strategic Partnerships Office that connects industry, academia, and other government agencies with center facilities, capabilities, specialized test environments, and technical expertise to bring ideas to life.

articles.title: PHP is in the foundation of 70% of websites – here’s what it is and why a flaw in the software is a major hacking threat
articles.dek: Governments and organizations around the world began scrambling on Oct.
paragraphs: Governments and organizations around the world began scrambling on Oct. 21, 2026, to fix a vulnerability in software that runs their websites, a bug that could give hackers access to data and control of websites. The flaw in PHP, the programming language that powers much of today’s web, prompted urgent warnings from the U. S. National Security Agency , cybersecurity agencies and software vendors.

A researcher at Calif , a security research firm, found the flaw in August 2026 using an advanced artificial intelligence model from OpenAI. The firm alerted the nonprofit that manages PHP. However, word of the flaw leaked before the PHP organization released patches for its software, and according to Amazon Web Services officials, hackers began “broadly” attempting to exploit it .

The vulnerability has implications far beyond a single company or platform, because PHP is a key piece of software that helps run millions of websites. So, what is PHP, what role did AI play in uncovering the vulnerability, and should the average user worry?

PHP is a programming language that powers most websites . For a modern website to provide dynamic content, visual elements and searchable features, a program must run on the web server and take user input, whether that is entering a web address or clicking links and buttons. Estimates suggest that around 70% of websites run on PHP.

PHP operates on a web server in two main parts : the core PHP system – the engine and runtime libraries – and the individual PHP scripts, which are the custom programs that actually implement a website. When you interact with a website, PHP scripts run, take user input and produce the output your web browser displays.

The current security issue sits directly in the core PHP system and the libraries it uses. When a vulnerability exists at this deep level, it can allow an adversary to exploit the system. In this case, they can run unauthorized commands on the computer hosting the website, which allows attackers to access data and gain full control of the website.

This vulnerability is not a mistake in an individual website’s code. The issue lies in the core PHP system, making every unpatched system running PHP vulnerable. Since websites are accessible to anyone on the internet, adversaries can easily find PHP-based websites using automated tools. From there, they can run an exploit program that takes advantage of the vulnerability.

This exploit code is called PHP2Shell. This name comes from the fact that the exploit gives the attacker “shell access,” a cybersecurity term for direct command-line control of the computer running the website. Shell access bypasses the website interface, giving adversaries a window to enter commands and access all the website’s data.

What makes this vulnerability particularly interesting is how it was discovered. This exploit came to light through a process known as coordinated disclosure, in which cybersecurity researchers report the flaw to PHP developers before publicizing it.

This discovery shows the power of AI in cybersecurity. For decades, finding subtle software flaws required large teams of specialists manually reviewing code. Today’s AI systems can examine vast codebases and identify unusual patterns in hours or days. These models can analyze millions of lines of code in seconds, spotting subtle memory management bugs that human auditors might miss over decades of software development. The PHP vulnerability has existed in the core PHP code for over a decade, and AI helped researchers find it.

However, this also shows that attackers can use these same tools to locate and exploit vulnerabilities. The same reasoning capabilities that help security researchers find flaws first can also let attackers rapidly scan the web for vulnerable targets and automate the creation of tools to exploit the vulnerabilities.
This illustrates why it is so critical for security teams to use AI to find vulnerabilities and report them safely and actively. AI can also help release patches that mitigate these vulnerabilities .

Many government agencies, universities, hospitals and businesses rely on PHP-based systems . While individual internet users are unlikely to be directly affected, organizations that delay patching could expose sensitive data, risk having their operations disrupted or give attackers a foothold into larger networks.
PHP runs entirely on remote web servers. If you are an everyday internet user visiting websites, you do not need to download a patch or fix your personal computer.

However, if you manage a website, blog or server, even a small site built on popular content management systems such as WordPress, you should check your server administration panel or web host immediately to ensure your PHP software is updated to the latest patched version. If a third party hosts your website, check with them to see whether they have patched for these vulnerabilities.

The PHP2Shell discovery illustrates a new reality for cybersecurity. In our interconnected world, keeping web infrastructure secure is a continuous race. As AI tools become standard for both cyber defenders and online adversaries, maintaining fast patching habits remains our most essential defense.

Doug Jacobson does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Why ultra-Orthodox parties hold so much sway in Israeli politics
articles.dek: On Oct. 20, 2026, a week before Israel’s elections, dozens of men were detained on suspicion of evading the draft – arrests that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called…
paragraphs: On Oct. 20, 2026, a week before Israel’s elections, dozens of men were detained on suspicion of evading the draft – arrests that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called “unacceptable .”

The young men attend ultra-Orthodox, or Haredi, religious schools, whose students were long exempt from the military service mandatory for most Israelis. A 2024 court ruling that Haredi men must be drafted alongside other Jewish youth intensified the conscription debate. Netanyahu’s government has failed to either legalize the draft exemption or enforce the court’s ruling, though he has said Haredim who are not studying should enlist .

With Israel’s military fighting in several conflicts, those exemptions have become increasingly unpopular: The vast majority of Jewish voters want Haredi communities to share the burden . Haredi political parties, however, are key potential coalition members as Netanyahu attempts to secure his political future. Although a relatively small percentage of the population, the Haredim hold disproportionate sway in Israel’s parliamentary system.

Haredi Jews strictly observe Jewish religious law and often disapprove of liberal interpretations. They typically live in Haredi-majority neighborhoods where large families are the norm – six children, on average – and about half of the men devote themselves to full-time religious study . The poverty rate is 33% , more than double the percentage for non-Haredi Jews.

The Israeli public is about 14% Haredi , but the community is growing quickly because of its high birth rate. Projections by the Central Bureau of Statistics estimate that almost a quarter of Israelis will be Haredi by 2050.

Haredi communities are diverse and represented by two main political parties. Haredim who are Ashkenazi – Jews whose ancestors came from northern and eastern Europe – are linked to United Torah Judaism, or UTJ. Those who are Sephardi or Mizrachi, meaning their ancestors came from the Iberian Peninsula and the Middle East, are linked to Shas.

A third Haredi party, Haredi Public, was formed in July 2026 . The party says it will represent Haredim who feel underserved by Shas and UTJ , emphasizing employment and poverty, housing development and the education system. Unlike the other two Haredi parties, it has included women on its candidate list.

Elections for the Israeli parliament, the Knesset, use a proportional representation system . Any party that receives more than 3. 25% of votes receives seats based on the fraction of votes it received. Each party allocates its seats to members based on a list of candidates published before elections.

Having multiple parties with similar target demographics risks dividing the vote, leaving that group with fewer representatives in the Knesset. Shas and UTJ have agreed to share their surplus votes in the 2026 election to maximize their overall seat share.

Because of the low electoral threshold, many parties are able to win seats. No Israeli party has ever attained the 50% share needed to control parliament by itself. As in other countries with similar systems, it is very common for parties to form coalitions and govern as a team.

Likud, one of the major conservative parties, has led most governing coalitions for the past two decades , with party leader Benjamin Netanyahu as prime minister. Haredi parties are seen as strong conservative allies , and they have been key coalition members for Likud administrations. Today, as Netanyahu faces challenges from other right-wing parties over his handling of Oct. 7, 2023, and several wars, Likud may need them even more.
The fact that Likud has needed Haredi parties to form coalitions has given them negotiating power. For many years, one of their priorities has been draft exemptions for religious education .

Military service is mandatory for most groups in Israel, although Muslim and Christian Arab citizens are generally exempted. Jewish Israelis see conscription as a unifying experience and a costly demonstration of commitment to the state. Starting at age 18, most women serve two years and most men serve almost three years. Former soldiers can be called up as reservists into their 40s, depending on their training.

For decades, Haredi men received de facto exemptions. It was, effectively, one of several government arrangements that subsidize Haredi communities. Religious schools for teen boys and married men receive government payments for each student. Given the communities’ low employment rates, large families and high poverty rates, many families rely on public support .

In 2024, Israel’s Supreme Court ruled that a blanket exemption from military service for Haredim was not legal . Netanyahu’s government struggled to enact a compromise between those who favored drafting Haredim and the Haredi parties; the failure to find a lasting legal way to exempt Haredi men led Shas and UTJ to leave the Likud-led coalition in 2025.
Nonetheless, this ruling has not led to mass conscription.

Haredi groups have held public protests , and many have ignored draft notices. While tens of thousands of men are draft eligible but not serving , and most of them are Haredi, fewer than 500 evaders have been arrested in 2026. Netanyahu argues against arrests , saying they discourage men from enlisting without coercion.

In July 2026, at the urging of Haredi parties, the government passed a law to temporarily prevent arresting draft evaders. Some members of Netanyahu’s governing coalition opposed the law, however, and right-wing opposition parties filed petitions to challenge it in court .

Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett – leader of the Together alliance, and seen as a key contender to oust Netanyahu – has threatened to cut subsidies to the Haredi community if they continue to defy the draft. Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the centrist Yashar party, is another top contender to replace Netanyahu . He has proposed allowing 3% of Haredi men exemptions to study , while drafting the majority.

As the number of conflict zones increases – Gaza, southern Lebanon and Iran, as well as deployments in the West Bank – the unequal burden of military participation is a growing source of resentment among many conscripted Israelis and their families. Seven in 10 Jewish Israelis favor drafting the Haredim.
Shas and UTJ, however, have declared they will not join a coalition unless it promises to codify the draft exemption into law .

When the Haredi parties exited Netanyahu’s coalition, Likud replaced them with nationalist parties that emphasize the state and Jewish supremacy. Particularly notable was the decision to include the Jewish Power party , an offshoot of an earlier group banned for racism ; including Kahanist groups was long seen as a red line .

Haredi communities, on the other hand, tend to prioritize religious Jewishness over the state. Most Haredim do not consider themselves Zionist , and a small percentage are anti-Zionist . They argue that it was sacrilegious for people to create a state of Israel rather than waiting for God to return Jews to the land of Israel. Where nationalist politicians emphasize the secular state and military service, Haredim see their religious study as service to the Jewish community.

As Likud’s changing coalition shows, Netanyahu’s alliances are strategic rather than ideological. I believe his decision to side with the Haredim on the recent draft legislation suggests his coalition is open to revision after the October 2026 election.

articles.title: Fear-based campaign ads can grab attention, but whether they win votes is less clear
articles.dek: On a Monday night in September 1964, television viewers watched a little girl counting petals on a flower.
paragraphs: On a Monday night in September 1964, television viewers watched a little girl counting petals on a flower. Her voice gave way to a man counting down, and then a nuclear blast filled the screen.

The ad ran as a paid spot only once , in support of President Lyndon B. Johnson’s reelection campaign. It never mentioned his opponent, republican Barry Goldwater . The ad played on a fear voters already held, that Goldwater might start a nuclear war . Republicans protested loudly, Democrats pulled the spot, and the uproar got it rebroadcast in full on network news.

I study how emotional appeals persuade, from how viewers’ moods shape their reactions to political ads to how anxiety drives people to seek out , and sometimes fail to absorb, information about threats.
The LBJ “Daisy” ad shows why political campaigns to this day continue to reach for fear , and it hints at why the payoff is less predictable than you might think.
Fear is an alarm . It tells you something threatening is close. You feel scared when you believe you are at risk from something dangerous that can hurt you.
Anxiety knocks people off autopilot, sharpens attention and sends them looking for new information. That heightened attentiveness may be exactly what a struggling campaign wants.

When political scientists Travis Ridout and Kathleen Searles tracked Senate ads from 2004, they found that front-runners often leaned on enthusiasm and pride in their messaging, while candidates who were behind leaned on fear and anger.

During the 1998 Massachusetts governor’s race, political scientist Ted Brader ran a study that embedded campaign ads in a news broadcast and changed only the music and images, keeping the words identical . Those changes produced completely different reactions. When a negative ad paired grainy black-and-white images of drug use with tense music, viewers paid closer attention to the spoken message and became more open to reconsidering their chosen candidate.

Fear cues – like a nuclear mushroom cloud – can push viewers to weigh fresh information and reconsider their choice. One surprise: Politically informed citizens were more responsive to these emotional cues than less engaged ones. Fear is not simply a tool for swaying the uninformed, undecided voter. It also reaches people who follow politics closely. Emotion provides the motivation, while knowledge provides the ability to think carefully about the issues and positions and seek out more information.

More broadly, a meta-analysis of over 100 studies found that fear appeals reliably shift attitudes and behavior across health and other domains. For instance, public health researcher Lucy Popova tested fear-based messages designed to discourage smokers from trying snus, a smokeless tobacco product. She found that when participants perceived a serious threat but also felt capable of acting on it, they held less favorable attitudes toward snus and were less inclined to try it.

Political attack ads – fear messaging being one type – have a shakier record. A review of more than 100 studies found no dependable evidence that negative campaigning wins elections, and some evidence that it lowers positive feelings toward the candidate who sponsors it.

Communication scholar Kim Witte’s research found that fear motivates action when people believe there is a workable response that they can carry out. When the threat feels big and the solution feels out of reach, people protect themselves from the message instead . They tune out, deny the threat or decide the messenger is the problem.

For example, picture an ad geared toward adolescent vaping that shows teens in hospital beds with ventilators using scary terms like “popcorn lungs.” If the ad also communicates that vaping can destroy lungs irreversibly, the teen audience is likely to experience extreme fear while at the same time feeling like there’s no way to fix the problem.

My colleagues and I have seen this effect in our own experiments. We found that people who felt highly anxious and also confident they could act sought out the most information . Those who felt anxious but lacked that confidence did go looking, yet they recalled very little. Anxiety pushed them to search but got in the way of absorbing what they read.
A campaign that frightens voters without offering a clear step to address the issue could end up producing plenty of anxious attention and very little learning.

Empowerment also helps explain who shows up at the polls. Political scientist Nicholas Valentino and colleagues found that anger boosted voter participation more reliably than anxiety, and anxiety mattered mainly for people who already had the skills and resources to take actions like donate to campaigns, attend rallies, sign petitions and so on.
Fear does its most reliable work when it attaches to a stereotype voters already carry. The 1988 presidential race provides two classic examples.

One controversial ad, produced in support of Republican George H. W. Bush, showed a mugshot of a Black man. The ad named the man, Willie Horton, and a voiceover explained that he’d committed rape and assault while on a weekend furlough from prison as part of a program run under Massachusetts Governor Michael Dukakis, the Democratic candidate. The spot linked fears about crime to race without saying so directly.

Bush’s campaign followed up with the “ Revolving Door ” ad, which built on that anxiety. It featured stark, black-and-white footage of inmates marching through a revolving gate while a narrator warned that Dukakis had let murderers out of prison on weekend passes.

Political scientist Tali Mendelberg’s research described in “ The Race Card ” shows that these implicit appeals to prejudices and fears are powerful . But they lose much of their force once someone publicly names them as racial. Implicit appeals work because they slip past most voters’ commitment to racial equality; once the racial message is pointed out, voters recognize it and many reject it rather than see themselves as endorsing prejudice.

In a national experiment, Public Policy researcher Mirya Holman and colleagues found that when campaign messages triggered fears of terrorism , voters turned to their stereotypes of strong leaders as masculine. Those stereotypes hurt a female Democratic candidate, while Republican candidates of either gender were unaffected, since Republicans are already seen as tough on security .

A message communicating a threat does not need to name a candidate’s identity to disadvantage them. It simply makes voters reach for the stereotypes they already hold. There’s less systematic research on candidates’ religion, though the same mechanism – fear pushing voters to rely on the stereotypes they already hold about who can keep them safe – predicts similar vulnerability for Muslim candidates .

In 1828, opponents accused presidential candidate Andrew Jackson of murder and cannibalism . Both parties have leaned on fear in the television era, from Reagan’s 1984 “ Bear ” ad about an unnamed Soviet threat, to Democrats’ 1996 warnings that seniors’ Medicare was at risk .

What has grown is negativity overall. Political scientist John Geer’s analysis of presidential ads from 1960 to 2004 documents that rise , though he also found attack ads, more likely than positive ones, to focus on real issues rather than personal traits. The evidence that fear specifically has increased, as opposed to negativity in general, is less clear.

articles.title: El Niño Then and Now
articles.dek: El Niño is part of a natural climate pattern that occurs roughly every two to seven years, bringing warmer-than-normal water to parts of the equatorial Pacific.
paragraphs: El Niño is part of a natural climate pattern that occurs roughly every two to seven years, bringing warmer-than-normal water to parts of the equatorial Pacific. The most recent very strong El Niño events, in 1997-98 and 2015-16, upended weather patterns. Impacts spanned the planet, from fires in Indonesia and the Amazon, to crop failures due to drought in southern Africa , to heavy rain and coastal flooding in Southern California. The current El Niño rivals these past heavyweights.

Every El Niño grows from a feedback loop between the atmosphere and the ocean. Trade winds normally keep warm water piled up in the western Pacific, where it stands higher than in the east. When those winds weaken, that warm water begins to pulse eastward, which further weakens and sometimes reverses the winds, allowing even more warm water to move east. The cycle intensifies as waters continue to warm and pile up in the central and eastern Pacific.

But each El Niño has its own character, shaped by where in the Pacific the warmth builds and how the atmosphere responds. “The search for the ‘typical’ El Niño is very elusive,” said Josh Willis, project scientist for sea level missions at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL). “They’re all different in terms of where they land and how their impacts play out.”

Altimetry satellites can track those differences by measuring the height of the sea surface. Because water expands as it warms, higher-than-normal sea levels in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific signal the buildup of heat associated with El Niño. The maps above depict sea surface height anomalies across the Pacific Ocean on October 13, 1997 (left), and on October 12, 2026 (right). Data are from the TOPEX/Poseidon satellite and the Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich satellite, respectively, and were processed by scientists at JPL.

Shades of red indicate where sea levels were higher than average. Normal sea level conditions appear white, and lower areas are blue. Signals related to seasonal cycles and long-term trends have been removed to highlight sea level anomalies associated with El Niño and other short-term natural phenomena.

“What’s unique about altimetry is that we have a 35-year record from nearly identical satellites flying almost the same ground track, with each mission overlapping the next,” Willis said. “That lets us look back in time and compare this El Niño to what happened in 1997. And right now, this one is on track to be even bigger.”

Compared with the 1997-98 event, El Niño in 2026 came on much more suddenly. But as of October, the two events appear similar in character—the tilt of sea level (low in the west and high in the east) and high, warm water extending all the way to South America—so Willis thinks the impacts could be similar as well. In 1997-98, that meant, for instance, lots of rain in California and across the southern tier of the U. S.

The 2015-16 El Niño was another heavy hitter but differed in its character. Sea surface height anomalies on October 12, 2015, based on altimetry data from the Jason-2 satellite, are shown above in context with maps from around the same time in 1997 and 2026. In 2015, the exceptionally warm, high water along the equator didn’t push up against South America to the extent it did in the other years. Rainfall impacts that winter concentrated more over Central America and the southeastern U. S. , with significant flooding in Mexico.

NOAA’s El Niño outlook on October 8, 2026, called for an 83 percent chance of a strong-to-very strong El Niño through the first three months of 2027. But exactly how the impacts will play out in winter 2026-27 and beyond remains to be seen. Willis noted that El Niño’s influence propagates through a chaotic atmosphere, and the signal can get muddled as it extends beyond the tropics. “There’s always a bit of a dice roll here,” Willis said. “Just because this El Niño looks like 1997 doesn’t mean it will be exactly the same—it’s just our best guess at the moment.”
NASA Earth Observatory maps by Lauren Dauphin, using NASA-SSH altimetry data provided by Josh Willis, Severine Fournier, and Kevin Marlis, NASA/JPL-Caltech.

articles.title: NASA Invites Media to 2026 von Braun Space Exploration Symposium
articles.dek: Members of the media are invited to join NASA at the 2026 von Braun Space Exploration Symposium from Monday, Oct. 26, to Wednesday, Oct.
paragraphs: Members of the media are invited to join NASA at the 2026 von Braun Space Exploration Symposium from Monday, Oct. 26, to Wednesday, Oct. 28, at the University of Alabama in Huntsville.
This year’s symposium is focused on humanity’s return to the Moon, sustainable lunar infrastructure, advanced space propulsion, and the evolving space workforce.

Panels include discussions on Artemis II and III, space propulsion flash talks, building utilities and infrastructure for sustainable lunar operations, Moon base supply chain resilience, space nuclear technology, navigating the new NASA workforce, and engineering the future, featuring keynotes and awards presentations.

To request an interview with NASA speakers during the event, media must contact Lance D. Davis, lance. d. davis@nasa. gov , and Joel Wallace, joel. w. wallace@nasa. gov . Media interested in participating in-person or online must contact the American Astronomical Society to register.

Organized by the American Astronautical Society in collaboration with NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, the annual event gathers leaders from government, industry, policy, and academia to discuss the current landscape of space exploration and help chart a path forward.

articles.title: Surviving cancer starts at diagnosis and continues after treatment – earlier survivorship care can help patients feel better and live longer
articles.dek: “You have cancer.” It’s a phrase that comes as a shock, then is quickly followed by a whirlwind of decisions that somehow feel fast and slow at the same time.
paragraphs: “You have cancer.” It’s a phrase that comes as a shock, then is quickly followed by a whirlwind of decisions that somehow feel fast and slow at the same time.

You have treatments to decide on. You are trying to figure out how you might work, care for your family and undergo a variety of intensive medical appointments all at the same time. You are centered on the here and now, and thinking about five or 10 years down the road is not at the forefront of your mind. Getting through treatment is the finish line you are reaching for; that is when you may actually feel like a cancer survivor.

As a nurse and scientist who has spent over a decade caring for cancer patients and studying ways to ease the effects of treatment, I have heard this story time and time again from both survivors and their loved ones. But survivorship actually begins at the time of diagnosis.

In fact, in our newly published research in JAMA Otolaryngology–Head & Neck Surgery, my team and I found that patients with head and neck cancer who started survivorship care – healthcare services that support a cancer survivor’s physical, emotional, social and practical needs – earlier were more likely to stick to treatment and be alive without cancer three years after treatment.

Clinicians and researchers consider a person a cancer survivor from the time they are diagnosed through the end of their life. More important than the term is what cancer survivorship is meant to look like for the patient.

Cancer survivorship reflects the patient’s experience with cancer and cancer treatment, and the physical, emotional and social effects that has on their life. Survivorship care is designed to identify and address the complex needs of a cancer survivor beyond just the physical changes. It involves coordinating care and promoting the person’s overall health and well-being.

This care can look different for each patient, depending on the cancer they have and their individual needs. For example, my team and I designed a survivorship clinic at UPMC in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, to address the most common issues head and neck cancer survivors experience. In addition to surgeons and nurses, our team includes swallowing therapists, a physical therapist, a dental care team and a dietitian to help address issues with swallowing, nutrition, dental health, physical function and mood. All of these services are offered at the same location and can be completed in one visit on the same day, generally under one copay.

After the visit, the cancer survivor, their oncology team and their primary care clinician receive a care plan to help coordinate care and communication among all their providers. Rather than as a one-time session, our survivorship clinic builds relationships with survivors, supporting them as their needs change over time.

While a person becomes a survivor at the time of diagnosis, most survivorship care is delivered after the initial treatment has ended. This may be partly because to be accredited by a major medical body that sets cancer care standards, the American College of Surgeons Commission on Cancer , hospitals must offer at least three services to cancer survivors after they complete their initial treatment.
While survivorship care can ease physical and psychological issues after cancer treatment, survivors often report significant unmet needs before and during treatment.

In my specialty of head and neck cancers, many patients undergo a grueling five to seven weeks of radiation therapy, often in addition to chemotherapy. They experience a host of side effects: pain, mouth sores, skin burns, difficulty swallowing and weight loss, which together can lead to treatment interruption and hospitalization . These side effects often continue and sometimes worsen years after treatment .

While our survivorship clinic was initially designed for patients who completed treatment, we later expanded our services to patients before radiation. We previously found that starting survivorship care before radiation was associated with better quality of life and reduced symptoms .

In our newly published research, we found that among 471 cancer survivors, 62% of those who attended our survivorship clinic before completing radiation finished treatment on time , compared with 48% of those who were not seen before completing radiation. At three years, 60% of patients seen in the survivorship clinic before completing radiation were alive and cancer-free, compared with 39% of those not seen before completion. The association remained after accounting for whether patients completed radiation on time, suggesting that on-time completion may not fully explain the difference.

Although our results suggest that shifting the start of survivorship care to before treatment may improve outcomes, they do not prove it. Our team plans to test in a larger clinical trial whether starting survivorship care before radiation helps patients finish treatment on time and maintain quality of life, while also examining how teams coordinate care and referrals.

Comprehensive cancer care implies not only a comprehensive treatment plan, but also supportive care that will help patients live well beyond their diagnosis and treatment. However, a 2024 survey of 384 facilities accredited by the American College of Surgeons Commission on Cancer found that only 1 in 5 programs estimated that most of their eligible patients receive survivorship care .

For head and neck cancer survivors specifically, nearly all clinicians routinely assess cancer recurrence, swallowing and thyroid function. But only about half address psychological symptoms , such as anxiety and depression, and fewer than 1 in 3 addressed body image or sleep problems.

Survivorship care is often framed as care that begins after treatment ends, which can delay patients’ access to support during treatment. Communication breakdowns may leave patients unaware of available services, while a lack of referrals can keep them from receiving needed care. Survivorship care also draws on clinicians with different areas of expertise, and some hospitals and treatment centers may lack enough dedicated staff time to provide a full range of services.
The end of treatment is a huge milestone that patients and their loved ones reach for. But it is not where survivorship care truly starts.

Making survivorship care more accessible may help make cancer care more comprehensive. Clinicians and researchers can start planning for the survivor’s life after cancer even when it’s not on the patient’s mind. Bringing a team that combines treatment experts with rehabilitation and supportive care specialists into the room early can help achieve better outcomes for patients.
As a cancer survivor or a loved one, you don’t need to wait.

Marci Lee Nilsen receives funding from the National Institutes of Health and the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation. She directs the UPMC Head and Neck Cancer Survivorship Clinic, which was the setting for the research described in this article.

articles.title: Indian Gen Z ‘cockroach’ protesters aim to upend assumptions about democracy – and populism – in Modi’s India
articles.dek: Five months after its founding , India’s Cockroach Janta Party, known as the CJP, has revealed what youth-led democratic movements can achieve – and how hard they are to sustain.
paragraphs: Five months after its founding , India’s Cockroach Janta Party, known as the CJP, has revealed what youth-led democratic movements can achieve – and how hard they are to sustain.

The movement was formed in May 2026 to protest the government’s cancellation of medical school entrance exams and after India’s Chief Justice Surya Kant likened unemployed youth to cockroaches. By July, the largely Gen Z movement had scored an early victory with the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

The CJP has since moved on to a much larger political issue: The Election Commission’s reported deletion of approximately 130 million names from the voter rolls. Since Oct. 2, protesters have descended on the streets of Delhi, Mumbai and other cities demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, halting the deletions pending an independent inquiry, and the restoration of the old electoral rolls before the next elections.

In the process, the CJP has encountered strong government resistance. Amid a crackdown on protests, two of the movement’s spokespersons – Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das – were detained , while Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his right-wing populist Bharatiya Janata Party, or BJP, have refused to bend on the voter roll issue – instead accusing protesters of undermining democracy.

Nonetheless, as a long-time scholar of Indian political parties and social movements , I believe the CJP’s protests have revealed people’s deep-seated anxieties over democratic erosion in a country of nearly 1. 5 billion. Through courage and acerbic wit, the CJP has done something that has eluded conventional opposition parties over the past 12 years: puncturing the ruling party’s aura of invulnerability . In doing so, I believe the protests have challenged the government’s view of who “the people” are, what democracy means, and who speaks for youth, women and the politically marginalized.

Modi often describes India as the “Mother of Democracy,” a reference to its civilizational heritage and to Bharat Mata, the Hindu mother goddess. Democracy, he insists, is not a Western import but a native inheritance. The implication is meant to be reassuring: India has always been democratic and always will be.

But some outside monitors disagree. Sweden’s V-Dem Institute classifies India as an “ electoral autocracy ,” meaning that although it regularly holds multiparty elections, it fails basic democratic benchmarks such as legislative and judicial checks and balances and citizens’ active political participation.
Judged by how the country treats dissent, the record is damning: using anti-terrorism laws to jail activists without trial , barricading protest sites, internet blackouts and police brutality .

By contrast, the CJP considers peaceful protest, along with upholding the country’s constitution, essential elements of democracy. Demonstrators regularly circulate images of B. R. Ambedkar – the chief architect of the Indian constitution – on posters, in slogans and in songs. Like Ambedkar, 30-year-old CJP leader Abhijeet Dipke is a Dalit, or untouchable within the Hindu caste system.

Critics argue that the BJP defines the nation through Hindu civilizational identity , which is exclusionary because it rejects India’s rich Muslim historical traditions and casts doubt on the political loyalties of the country’s Muslims, who constitute about 14% of the population – 197 million people. By contrast, the CJP draws no line between insider and outsider by faith, caste or birth, and it defines community by shared commitments.

The voter roll struggle shows what is at stake in the question. The Election Commission says the revision will remove duplicate entries, deceased voters and noncitizens . But critics worry that the burden of proof falls on voters. Consider how hard it is for poor Muslims, Dalits and migrant workers to produce decades-old birth, education and land certificates. Moreover, those whose names are struck from the electoral rolls fear being branded illegal immigrants .
While the BJP had held the prime minister’s office before, Modi’s 2014 election marked a sea change in Indian politics, disrupting the Congress Party’s dominance.

The BJP owed it electoral success in part to attracting young and first-time voters with promises of employment, economic growth and what is known in Hindi as “ achhe din aane waale hain ,” or “good days are coming.” Since the BJP took office in 2014, the country has charted strong GDP growth, but the macroeconomic success has been belied by ongoing and rampant inequality that falls especially hard on the poor and young.

The BJP claims to have fulfilled some of its more targeted campaign promises, such as engaging in merit-based public sector hiring . Yet 40% of Indian college graduates under 25 are unemployed . Paradoxically, the unemployment rate for youth who cannot read and write hovers around just 3. 4%. For college graduates, who are the CJP’s main constituency, it is nearly nine times higher at roughly 29% .

Seizing on this building discontent, the CJP uses the slogan “Achhe Din” ironically, on posters and memes. Its manifesto opens: “If you are going to call us cockroaches, the least you can do is pay our rent.” It calls for making “lazy” – a code word for the unemployed – a protected political identity.

Underlying the joke is a serious point: that stigmatization of the jobless offends millions of impoverished people, something critics note is protected in the dignity and equality guarantees of articles 21 and 14 of the Constitution.

The BJP has gained women’s electoral support through a combination of targeted welfare schemes, support for increased women’s representation in legislatures and endless talk of women’s empowerment, or “nari shakti .”
However, masses of women protesters have challenged state-defined women’s empowerment. They stop police vans carrying detainees, scale barricades and criticize the prime minister.

One of the most prominent among them is Neha Bora, a Ph. D. student and president of the left-wing All India Students’ Association, whose blunt messages to Modi has seen her profile skyrocket. Modi has said he has been subject to vulgar abuses by the protesters and was shocked by how “our daughters” could use such foul language, but he viewed them as “misdirected children” and was ready to forgive them .

The throngs of women who are protesting express deep discontent with the government’s paternalism. They challenge its Hindu-inflected understanding of empowerment and insist on speaking for themselves rather than being spoken for. They express outrage at the government’s brutal response to their peaceful protests. They describe how the police have beaten and sexually harassed them, while anonymous self-styled guardians of religious morality engage in doxing, threats of rape and acid attacks, and circulate demeaning AI-generated images of them. For protesters, that record sits uneasily besides the prime minister’s denunciation of violence against women .

The CJP motto, “Cockroaches never die,” has wide resonance. Protesters have survived, but not escaped, violence, incarceration, internet blackouts and police blockades. The sunglass-wearing cockroach mascot makes a mockery of leader-centered nationalist branding.

Recent youth-led uprisings in Bangladesh and Nepal have shown how quickly online mobilization can outrun official control. What distinguishes the CJP is that it pairs humor with legal and technical infrastructure. Its online portal Saakshi vault , which means “witness,” collects photos and videos of police violence that protesters upload; volunteer lawyers use these to issue complaints against officers.

The CJP’s recent and remarkable successes do not mean that the movement is likely to disrupt the BJP’s hold on power in the next parliamentary elections in 2029. For now at least, the CJP is fairly concentrated in urban strongholds and would need to build organizational infrastructure and develop long-term demands.

However, a generation that a government minister wrote off as lazy and expendable has exposed the cracks in the system that the chief justice defended. Whatever form it takes, the movement provides a vision and reminder of what democracy looks like.
